lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man and an enrolments officer at a community college. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good afternoon, Northgate Community College, enrolments. Rachel speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, hello. I'm ringing about the evening classes — the autumn ones. Is it too late to sign up?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Not at all. We've still got places on most of them. Have you studied with us before?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: No, this'd be my first time.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, then I'll need to put you on the system. Could I take your surname first?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's Okafor.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sorry, would you mind spelling that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Of course. O. K. A. F. O. R. Okafor.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Lovely, thank you. And your first name?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Daniel.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thanks, Daniel. And could I have an address?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Yes, it's twenty-seven Bellfield Road. Bellfield — that's B. E. L. L. F. I. E. L. D. — Road, Northgate.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twenty-seven Bellfield Road. Got it. And are you working at the moment? I only ask because a few of our courses have a daytime group as well.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Yes, I'm an electrician, so honestly the evening is the only thing that works for me.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's no problem at all — nearly all the craft courses run in the evening. Can I also ask how you heard about us? We have to report it for our funding.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Erm, I think I saw something on your website first. No — actually, that's not right. I picked up one of your brochures in the library.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The library, perfect. They're very good to us. So, did you have a particular course in mind?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Well, I was hoping to do Introduction to Photography, but a mate of mine said it's already full.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I'm afraid he's right — photography filled up in about a week. There's still room on Introduction to Bookbinding, though, and it's the same tutor.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Bookbinding. Do you know, that actually sounds better. Put me down for that one, please.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Introduction to Bookbinding. Now, that course runs twice a week — there's a Tuesday group and a Thursday group.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Tuesday would be — hmm, no, sorry, I've got five-a-side on Tuesdays. Thursday, please.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thursday it is. I'll email a confirmation across once we're finished.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, Daniel, just a few practical things. The Thursday group meets in the Beech Building, on the first floor.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And what time does it start? I don't finish work until six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You'll be fine. We used to begin at half past six, but we pushed it back — classes now start at 6.45 and run through until nine.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: 6.45. That gives me time to get across town. And what about the fee?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the full fee for a ten-week term is 96 pounds.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Ah. Right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But there's a reduced rate for anyone living in the borough, and Bellfield Road is well inside it, so you'll pay 86 pounds a term.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's a relief. Can I pay it in instalments?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can — two payments. One when you enrol, and one at half term.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Great. And is there anything I need to buy beforehand? Tools, or a kit of some sort?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No, all the tools stay in the workshop. People often turn up with their own scissors and a bone folder, but we supply all of that. The one thing I would say is bring an apron, because the glue does splash.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: An apron. I'll dig one out of the van.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And do bring your enrolment reference to the first session. It'll be at the bottom of the email.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Will do. Can I ask what happens if I have to miss a week? We sometimes get called out at short notice.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's fine — just let the tutor know. She puts a short summary of each session on the course page, so you can catch up before the next one. As long as you make eight of the ten, you'll get your certificate.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, there's a certificate? I wasn't expecting that.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There is, and there's a little exhibition on the last Thursday of term — families are welcome. Most people bring whatever they've made.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That sounds lovely. Right — oh, one last thing: parking. Is there anywhere to leave the van?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There is, yes. The main car park is reserved for staff during the day, and at weekends it's closed for the market — but from six in the evening it's free for anyone on a course.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Perfect. That's everything, I think. Thanks very much for your help, Rachel.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You're welcome, Daniel. We'll see you on the fifth of October.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one.

questions.prompt:
NORTHGATE COMMUNITY COLLEGE — ENROLMENT FORM
Surname: ______
questions.explanation: The printed word 'Surname' tells you before the audio that this is transcription, not comprehension. 'Would you mind spelling that for me' is the cue to stop listening for meaning. He says the name, then gives six letters. No trap: the whole mark is orthography. Write the letters as they land.

questions.prompt: Address: 27 ______ Road, Northgate
questions.explanation: '27' and 'Road' are already printed, so predict one word: a street name, spelled. 'Could I have an address' announces it a turn early. He says the whole address, then spells the middle word only. No trap. Write the nine letters and leave 'Road' alone.

questions.prompt: Occupation: ______
questions.explanation: 'Occupation' wants a job noun, singular, no article. She never says the word: she asks whether he is working. He answers with the trade in his first clause. Clean item. Write the noun, not the verb, and not the employer.

questions.prompt: Heard about the college from: a brochure in the ______
questions.explanation: 'a brochure in the' wants a singular place, and 'the' is already printed. He answers, then withdraws it: 'No — actually, that's not right.' The website is the value he takes back; the library is the one he leaves standing. One word, no article.

questions.prompt: Course chosen: Introduction to ______
questions.explanation: 'Introduction to' is printed, so predict one word: a craft. 'There's still room on' is the offer, one turn before he accepts. He asks for photography and is refused; the course he says yes to is the one that goes on the form. Write it as one word.

questions.prompt: Class day: ______ evenings
questions.explanation: 'evenings' is printed, so predict a weekday. 'hmm, no, sorry' is the repair marker and it lands mid-sentence. He starts on Tuesday, gives his reason for refusing it, then names the day he wants. The last day stated for the slot is the answer. Singular.

questions.prompt:
Practical details
Classes start at ______ (until 9 p.m.)
questions.explanation: 'until 9 p.m.' is printed, so predict a start time only. 'we pushed it back' is the repair marker. Half past six is given in the past tense and replaced in the same sentence. A time in the past tense never answers a present-tense timetable. Write the figure alone.

questions.prompt: Fee Daniel will pay per term: £______
questions.explanation: The pound sign is printed, so predict a bare figure in the tens. 'But there's a reduced rate' is the contrast that carries the answer. Two prices arrive seconds apart; the stem asks what Daniel pays, not what the course costs. Write the second figure only.

questions.prompt: What does Rachel tell Daniel to bring to the workshop?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect all three items to be spoken. 'The one thing I would say is' marks the endorsed one. Scissors and a bone folder are named as things people bring, then cancelled by 'we supply all of that'. Only the apron survives. Write A, not the word.

questions.prompt: Course members can park in the main car park
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect every time of day to be named. 'one last thing: parking' announces the topic a turn early. Daytime is for staff and weekends are closed for the market, so both wrong options are stated as true facts about other times. Only the evening is open to members.

parts.title: Welcome talk at the Fairhaven Leisure Centre

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a duty manager giving a welcome talk to a group of new members at a leisure centre. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hi everyone, and welcome to Fairhaven. My name's Marissa, I'm one of the duty managers here, and this little talk is what we do instead of a guided tour — mainly because the tour takes forty minutes and the coffee is free for the next twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, a bit of history first, because somebody always asks what this building used to be. Most people guess it was already a swimming pool. It wasn't. And it wasn't the old cinema either — that was two streets over, where the car showroom is now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: This was the town's bus depot, right up until 2019.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can still see it, actually. That high curved roof over the main pool is the original depot roof, and the green tiles in the entrance hall came straight out of the old ticket office.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. The practical things. Your membership card is also your locker key — tap it on the locker door to lock, tap it again to open. If you lose it, a replacement is four pounds, so please try not to.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You really don't need to bring much with you. Towels are free to borrow: just ask at reception and drop them in the basket by the exit on your way out.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Swimming costumes and goggles you would have to buy, I'm afraid, and the vending machine by the door is honestly a last resort.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Parking is the thing I get asked about most. When we first opened we only had ninety spaces and it was chaos every evening, but the extension last spring took us up to 120, plus twelve accessible bays right beside the door.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The barrier reads your number plate, so there's nothing for you to do. The first three hours are free as long as your card has been scanned inside the building.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, the pool timetable is printed on the back of your welcome sheet, but let me flag one thing, because people get this wrong all the time. If you don't like a crowded pool, everybody assumes Saturday morning is the quiet one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It really isn't — Saturday morning is when the swimming club has all six lanes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Our quiet swim sessions are on Sunday mornings, seven until ten. Lane ropes out, no whistles, and the lights are kept low. It's the nicest two hours of the week, in my opinion.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And bookings. Anything with an instructor — classes, the squash courts, the climbing wall — has to be booked through the app. Not the website.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The website is only for memberships, and it will cheerfully tell you a class is available when it's been full since Tuesday. So: the app.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Booking opens a week ahead at seven in the morning, and yes, the popular classes do go in about two minutes.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. The last thing I want to do is point a few of you in the right direction, because Fairhaven is a big building and it's very easy to end up doing exactly the same thing every week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So — if you've never actually learnt to swim, and a lot of adults haven't, there's nothing unusual about it at all, please don't start in the main pool. It's two metres deep at the shallow end and it's full of people doing lengths.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Go to the learner pool instead, round behind the changing rooms. It's warmer, it's chest-deep the whole way along, and there's an instructor in the water every weekday evening.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you're training for something, on the other hand — and we've got a lot of members doing the half marathon in October — the treadmills upstairs will do you no favours whatsoever. Use the outdoor track.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's floodlit until nine, it's properly measured, and on Tuesday evenings there's a group that runs intervals together.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then there are people who simply cannot make themselves exercise alone. I'm one of them, honestly. If that's you, the studio is where you want to be.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There are eighteen classes a week in there, everything from spin to very gentle chair yoga, and you'll be in a room with thirty other people who also didn't want to come.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you're bringing small children in, particularly at lunchtime, then it's the family café on the first floor. There's a play corner, the floor is designed to be dropped on, and nobody minds the noise.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The roof terrace is lovely, but that's the one place we ask people to keep the tables adult-only until two o'clock.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if what you actually want is to try something you have genuinely never done before — the climbing wall. You do need a twenty-minute induction first, that's free, and after that you can book it like anything else.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One of our members started at seventy-one, so I don't want to hear about your knees.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's me finished. Grab a coffee, have a wander round, and if you get lost — and everyone gets lost near the squash courts — just ask anybody in a red top.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two.

questions.prompt:
FAIRHAVEN LEISURE CENTRE — NEW MEMBERS
The building was previously the town's ______.
questions.explanation: 'the town's' is printed, so predict a building type and no article of your own. She names the two buildings people guess and cancels both before the answer arrives. 'It wasn't' is the whole cancellation and it is spoken quietly. Two words, no article.

questions.prompt: Members can borrow ______ free of charge.
questions.explanation: 'borrow' plus 'free of charge' predicts a plural thing you take and give back. 'You really don't need to bring much with you' announces the whole list. Towels are free; costumes and goggles are named a line later as things you must buy. One plural word.

questions.prompt: Number of parking spaces since the extension: ______
questions.explanation: 'since the extension' predicts a bare count and tells you a second, earlier figure exists. 'took us up to' is the cue. Three numbers arrive in one sentence: ninety before, 120 after, twelve accessible bays on top. Write the figure that follows 'up to' and nothing else.

questions.prompt: Quiet swim sessions: ______ mornings, 7-10 a.m.
questions.explanation: 'mornings' plus a printed time predicts a day of the week. 'Our quiet swim sessions are on' is the cue. Saturday is named twice with the word 'quiet' attached to it, then contradicted outright. Write the day that follows 'It really isn't', in the singular.

questions.prompt: Classes and courts must be booked using the ______.
questions.explanation: 'using the' predicts a singular thing you book through, with the article already printed. 'has to be booked through' is the cue. Two candidates are named within seconds and the website is cancelled twice, first by 'Not the website' and then by 'only for memberships'.

questions.prompt: someone who has never learnt to swim
questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and note that she opens every recommendation with the type of person, not the place. 'please don't start in the main pool' is a negation, which tells you the main pool is the wrong letter before the right one arrives. The learner pool follows 'instead'.

questions.prompt: someone training for a race
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the indoor option to be raised first. 'on the other hand' opens the item and the treadmills are dismissed in the same sentence they are named in. The recommendation is the imperative that follows: 'Use the outdoor track.'

questions.prompt: someone who cannot exercise on their own
questions.explanation: Predict a letter. 'If that's you' is the cue and it comes one clause before the place. She describes the person for two sentences before naming anything, which is the pattern for every item in this group. Nothing is offered and withdrawn here: it is a clean item.

questions.prompt: someone eating with young children
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect two places that suit children. 'If you're bringing small children in' is the cue. The café is named with its play corner; the roof terrace is named immediately afterwards and fenced off for adults until two. An exclusion spoken quietly still kills the option.

questions.prompt: someone who wants to try an activity that is new to them
questions.explanation: Predict a letter. The stem's phrase is 'new to them' and she paraphrases it as 'something you have genuinely never done before' before naming anything. The place follows the dash. Clean item, and the last of the five: any letter still blank should be guessed now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two geography students, Priya and Callum, discussing a field-work project with their tutor, Doctor Hallam. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Come in, both of you. Right — the field-work proposal. I've read it. Before we get into the detail, tell me what happened to the river study, because that's what you pitched to me last month.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Yes, sorry, we did change it. We were going to sample water quality along the Cray, but when we went to book the meters, the second-year group had already taken all four of them for the whole of March.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We did ask whether we could borrow a set from the university across town, but their technician said no. Insurance, apparently.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's a shame. Honestly, though, it's not a disaster — you'd have spent half your word count explaining the chemistry. So now it's air quality on the high street.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's right. Nitrogen dioxide, using diffusion tubes, and then a short questionnaire with pedestrians about whether they actually notice the traffic.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Mm. I like the questionnaire. What worries me is the measurement side. Talk me through where the tubes are going.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Six sites. Three at the pedestrianised end by the market, and three at the junction outside the station.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Six sites is fine. That isn't what I mean. Look at your timings — you've got every tube going up at nine in the morning and coming down at five the same afternoon.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Well, that's a full working day.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It is. But it's one working day. Nitrogen dioxide doesn't sit still — you'll catch a rush-hour spike, a lunchtime dip, and if it happens to rain on your Tuesday you'll have measured the weather, not the traffic.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Diffusion tubes are designed to run for a fortnight.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: So we just leave them up for two weeks.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Two weeks minimum, and take them down at the same hour you put them up. That one change will do more for your marks than anything else in this proposal.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's fine by us — it actually makes life easier. We were dreading a fourteen-hour day in February.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Now. The questionnaire. How long is it at the moment?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Twenty-two questions.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Twenty-two. And how long did it take you to fill in?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: About seven minutes.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And you wrote it. Nobody standing outside a chemist's in February is going to give you seven minutes.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We could always put it online instead — a QR code in the shop windows.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You could, but then you lose the one thing that makes it field work: you, standing there, watching who walks past. No — cut it. Five questions, one side of paper, and you'll get four times the responses.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Five. All right. We'd keep the two about perceived noise, and the one about how they travelled in.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Can I raise the other thing that's bothering me? I'm not convinced we'll get a representative sample at all. Half the people on that high street on a weekday are commuters walking from the station car park to the platform.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: They don't live in the borough, they've got no particular view about local air quality, and they're in a hurry.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's a genuinely good observation — and it's a finding, not a problem. Make 'where have you come from today' your first question, and then you can report your results by group.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Residents notice it, commuters don't: that's a far more interesting paragraph than anything you'd get out of twenty-two questions.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Should we be comparing our numbers with anything official?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You should — and that's actually where I'd start, before you order a single tube. The council publishes an annual air-quality report, and there's been a permanent monitoring station on that junction since 2016.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Read the last three years of it, take their baseline, then design your sites so they tell us something the station can't.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The journal literature can wait until you write your discussion, and you've clearly read the department handbook already — your risk assessment was the best I've seen this term.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. Let's divide the work up, because you've got three weeks and a reading week sitting in the middle of them. Who's doing what?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I'll take the tubes. I've already emailed the lab and they've got twelve spare, so I'll book those out on Monday and get them labelled.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Good. And the council data?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's me. My cousin works in the planning office — which doesn't help in the slightest, but at least I know who to ask. I'll request the raw monthly figures rather than the summary table.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Ask by email, so you've got a record of what you requested. And the risk assessment will need redoing now the tubes are staying up for a fortnight — different hazards, and you'll be working up a ladder on the lamp posts.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's mine as well, then. I wrote the first one, so I may as well.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Fine. The questionnaire itself?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We thought we'd write that one together, actually. We disagree about half the wording, so it's probably better if we argue it out now rather than in the write-up.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It is. And we'll both pilot it — ten people each, on the Saturday.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's the right instinct. And the mapping? I want to see your sites on a proper base map, not a screenshot of an online one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I'll do the maps. I took the mapping module last year, so I can get the traffic-flow layer in underneath as well.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And I'll draft the method section while she's doing that.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Send me one page a week. Not a polished draft — one page, in whatever state it's in. That's the only thing that keeps a project like this on schedule.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thank you. That's really helpful.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: See you next Tuesday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three.

questions.prompt: The students abandoned their river study because
questions.explanation: The stem asks why they abandoned the study, not what the tutor thought of it. 'tell me what happened to the river study' announces it a turn early. Priya gives the reason at once: the meters were all booked. The tutor's opinion arrives later and answers a different question.

questions.prompt: What does Dr Hallam see as the main weakness of the measurement plan?
questions.explanation: Expect the tutor to name what is fine before he names what is wrong. 'Diffusion tubes are designed to run for a fortnight' is the verdict. He accepts the six sites explicitly, then says 'That isn't what I mean', which is the moment option A dies. The weakness is the single day.

questions.prompt: Dr Hallam advises the students to
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and watch who proposes what. Callum offers the QR code; the stem asks what Dr Hallam advises. 'No — cut it' is the decision marker and the instruction follows in the same breath. An option raised by the wrong speaker is still the wrong option.

questions.prompt: What is Callum worried about?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and note the stem names Callum, so track the male student's turns. 'Can I raise the other thing that's bothering me' announces his worry explicitly. He then states it in two sentences: the pedestrians are commuters who do not live in the borough. Clean item, no reversal.

questions.prompt: Dr Hallam tells the students to begin by reading
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect all three readings to be named. 'that's actually where I'd start' is the endorsement and it lands on the council report. The journal literature is deferred to the discussion and the handbook is already read, so both are cancelled in one sentence at the end.

questions.prompt: booking the diffusion tubes
questions.explanation: Predict a letter, A, B or C, and track the voices rather than the words. 'Who's doing what?' opens the whole set. Priya claims the tubes in her first clause, in the first person, and backs it with what she has already done. A task named by the tutor is not a task claimed.

questions.prompt: obtaining the council's monitoring data
questions.explanation: Predict a letter. 'And the council data?' is the tutor naming the task one turn early, which is the pattern for every item here. Callum claims it with 'That's me' before he says anything else. The cousin in the planning office is a joke, not a second person doing the job.

questions.prompt: rewriting the risk assessment
questions.explanation: Predict a letter. The tutor raises the task without naming an owner: 'the risk assessment will need redoing'. Callum takes it in the next turn with a reason. Nothing is contested, so this is a clean item, but the ownership is decided a full turn after the task word is spoken.

questions.prompt: drafting the questionnaire
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the shared option to be used at least once. 'The questionnaire itself?' names the task. Priya answers with 'we' rather than 'I', and gives the reason: they disagree about the wording. Callum confirms it in the next turn. This is the only genuinely joint task.

questions.prompt: preparing the maps
questions.explanation: Predict a letter. 'And the mapping?' names the task one turn early. Priya claims it with 'I'll do the maps' and gives her reason. Callum then says he will draft the method 'while she's doing that' - a second task in the same sentence, and the commonest place to lose this item.

parts.title: Lecture: street trees and the modern city

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about street trees in cities. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good morning. Last week we looked at parks, which are essentially pieces of countryside that a city has agreed to keep. This week I want to talk about something much stranger: the tree that lives in the pavement. The street tree.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And I want to start with where the idea came from, because it isn't ancient. Medieval cities had orchards inside the walls, and they had a tree on the green, but they did not line their streets with trees.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The deliberate planted avenue is a Renaissance invention, and the first city to do it at any scale was Paris, in the sixteen hundreds.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: London followed a century later, and Berlin later still, and in both cases the model was explicitly the Parisian one — a straight road, a double row of limes, and a view at the end of it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, why? If you ask people today why the Victorians planted street trees, they'll usually say for beauty, or for the birds. Neither is right, and the second one would have puzzled them enormously.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The reason given in almost every council minute of the eighteen sixties is shade. Shade for pedestrians, shade for horses, and shade for the shop fronts, because sunlight faded the goods in the window. It's a completely practical argument.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There was a second argument, though, and it's the one I find most interesting, because it was wrong. Before germ theory was accepted, the great fear in cities was bad air — miasma. And trees, it was believed, cleaned that air and therefore prevented disease.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There are pamphlets from the cholera years that recommend planting as a public-health measure, in the same paragraph as widening the sewers.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: They were wrong about the mechanism, obviously. But we'll come back to whether they were wrong about the outcome.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right — species. If you walk down almost any older street in a British or French city and look up, you're probably looking at one tree: the London plane. And the plane was not chosen because anybody thought it was beautiful. It was chosen because it survives.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It tolerates industrial air, it doesn't mind having its roots in rubble, and it sheds its bark in plates, which takes the soot off with it — a self-cleaning tree, in a city that burned coal.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Where the plane failed, cities moved to limes, and then to a much wider palette after the disease outbreaks of the last thirty years taught us what a monoculture costs.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But survival is exactly where the modern problem lies. The average street tree planted today in a British city has a life expectancy, in some surveys, of under twenty years. A plane in a park will live for three hundred.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So what kills them? Not, usually, pollution, and not vandalism, although both get blamed. The single commonest cause of early death is compaction.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The soil under a pavement is compacted to something close to the density of concrete, deliberately, because that's what stops the paving from moving.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Roots cannot get air or water through it, and a tree that cannot root simply declines for a decade and then dies in a dry summer.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which brings us to what we now ask these trees to do — and we ask a great deal more of them than the Victorians did.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first thing is temperature. A street with a closed canopy can be five degrees cooler at head height, on a summer afternoon, than the identical street next to it without trees.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: In a city with an ageing population and no air conditioning, that is not a comfort question, it's a mortality question — which is, I think, the sense in which the miasma pamphlets accidentally got it right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The second is water. A mature canopy intercepts rainfall before it reaches the drains, and the fashionable engineering solution now is to plant trees in structural soil that doubles as a storm-water reservoir. The tree becomes part of the drainage system.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the third is money, which is where management comes in. Once you can put a figure on the cooling and the drainage and the particulates, a tree stops being decoration on the balance sheet and becomes an asset — and assets have to be replaced.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Most local authorities are now required to publish a replanting programme, setting out how many trees they will put back for each one they take down.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The public dimension of this is worth a moment. When Melbourne mapped its urban forest, it gave every single tree an identification number and, as an afterthought, an email address, so that residents could report damage.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: What happened instead is that people wrote to the trees. Thousands of letters — some of them, I promise you, love letters. Which tells you something useful about consent: it is much harder to fell a tree that people have written to.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, targets, and then I'll stop. The figure you'll see in most strategy documents is a canopy-cover target of thirty per cent — that is, thirty per cent of the city's surface shaded when you look down on it from above. Very few European cities are there.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The typical British figure is around sixteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the constraint on getting there is changing. For a century the limiting factor on urban planting was pollution, and we solved a great deal of that. The limiting factor now, on every species list I've read in the last five years, is drought.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The question is no longer what a tree can breathe, it's what it can drink.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Next week we'll look at how you actually value one of these things in cash terms, and I'll ask you to bring the two valuation papers from the reading list.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man booking a holiday cottage and an assistant at a letting office. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Good morning, Penvale Cottages, Ruth speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh, morning. I'm ringing about the self-catering places you do. We're after a week in the spring, if there's anything left.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There is, yes, plenty. Spring's a good deal quieter than the summer for us. Let me open a booking form and take a few details off you. Can I start with a surname?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's Whitlow.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sorry, would you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Course. W. H. I. T. E. No, sorry, ignore that, there's no E in it. Let me start again. W. H. I. T. L. O. W. Whitlow.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Whitlow. Right, I've got that.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And a number we can get you on in the daytime?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's oh one four seven two, double three oh, nine one five.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh one four seven two, double three oh, nine one five. Lovely, thank you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And how many of you would there be?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Just the two of us this time. We're leaving the children with their grandmother, which is honestly the whole idea of the trip.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Two adults, then. And when were you thinking of coming down?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The week beginning the fourteenth of April, if that's still free.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Let me have a look for you. The fourteenth of April. No, I'm afraid that one went on Friday. I could do you the week after, the twenty-first.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The twenty-first is fine. Better for us, if anything, because my brother isn't back from sea until the Wednesday.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The twenty-first it is. Now, I've got two cottages free that week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's Larkspur, which is the one down by the river with the veranda, and there's Bramble, up behind the farmhouse.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Does either of them take a dog?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Bramble does. Larkspur's got the better view, I'll be honest with you, but it's the one with the steps down to it, and we don't allow dogs in that one at all.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then it'll have to be Bramble. The dog is the entire point of the holiday, according to my wife.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Bramble, then. I'll pencil you in. Now, there's a deposit to hold it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: How much are we talking?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's normally a hundred and twenty pounds. But you're booking more than eight weeks ahead, and when people do that it comes down to ninety.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Ninety. That's manageable.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And you get it back afterwards, obviously, so long as nothing's broken and the place isn't left in a state.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, a few practical things and then I'll let you get on. Keys.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Do we have to come into the office for those?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can, but it's a twenty-minute drive out of your way. Mrs Ackroyd next door used to keep a spare set for us, only she's moved now. So what everybody does these days is the key safe on the wall by the back door. I'll text you the code the night before.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's easier all round.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Much. Now, parking. There's room for one car right outside Bramble, and for most people that's plenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you bring a second one, though, it goes in the yard by the farmhouse. And I'd ask you not to leave it on the lane, because the milk lorry can't get past.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: One outside, one in the yard if we need it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's it. Then the heating, which does catch people out in April. There's a wood burner in the sitting room and a basket of logs in the porch, and that first basket comes with the cottage. After that there's an honesty box on the shelf.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And if we get through more than that?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Couple of pounds in the box and help yourself. Some people bring their own down in the car, which is fine, though it's a lot to carry for what it costs.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Could we order more through you?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We're not a shop, I'm afraid. The garage out on the main road does bags of kindling, if you're ever desperate.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Last thing, and then I'll let you go. Check-out is ten o'clock on the Saturday, and we ask everyone to strip the beds and leave the linen in the basket on the landing. You don't need to hoover or scrub anything, because there's a cleaner in that morning.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the towels?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: In the same basket, please. Whatever you do, don't put those through the machine yourselves. The last lot came out grey and I had to buy forty new ones.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Message received. That's all very clear, thank you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You're very welcome. I'll email the confirmation across within the hour, and there's a little map on the back of it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Opening the Marlow Valley Science Weekend

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear the organiser of a country science weekend opening the event in front of visitors and volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fourteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Morning, everyone, and thanks for turning up this early on a long weekend. I'm Alison, I chair the committee, and I get ten minutes before the first session, so I'll be quick and you can all get a coffee.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A bit of history, because most of you weren't here at the start. This whole thing began as a school project. It was Year eleven — sorry, no, Year 12, I always get that wrong. A group of Year 12 students who wanted to put the telescope somewhere people could actually use it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And it has grown, frankly, beyond what any of us planned. We told the council two thousand people in the grant application, and I remember thinking that was ambitious. Last year we counted just over three thousand through the gates across the two days.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Money. Almost none of it costs you anything. The bus out to the observatory is the one thing you pay for? It's ten dollars a seat, that's the diesel and nothing else, and you book it on the desk at the door, not on your mobile.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Volunteers now. We did hand out those bright orange vests for a couple of years and, look, nobody wore them, so we've stopped. What every volunteer does need is a lanyard from the front desk, because that's what gets you into the back of the pavilion.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. That's the boring half done. The interesting half is where everything actually is, because we have spread ourselves all over this town.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So. Six venues, which for a town this size is showing off a bit. The main exhibition is in the showground pavilion, that has never moved and it never will, and the teachers' session is in there too on the Sunday, same as every year.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The solar car races are down on the tennis courts, both afternoons. Sixteen cars this year, most of them built at the TAFE, and the thing people always say afterwards is that you cannot hear a single one of them coming. Which is very much the point of a solar car.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, the primary school is where the under-fives go. There is a colouring-in table in the pavilion as well and every year somebody sits their toddler down at it and waits, but the actual little kids' program, the water tables and the bubbles and the mud kitchen, that's all up at the school.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Astronomy. Obviously that one can't start until it's properly dark, and the only big flat unlit space in this town is the bowls club green. So the telescopes go on the green, from about half past eight, and the bowls club has very kindly agreed not to mind.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The rocket launches used to be behind the school, and we had, let's say, several conversations about that with the neighbours. So this year the launches are at the fire shed, out on the highway, where nobody lives and there is a fire truck sitting right there.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the microscope lab is in the old bank. Lovely room, gorgeous ceiling, and it holds twelve people. Twelve. So that is the only session on the whole program where you have to put your name down first, and the list is on the desk by the front door.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Parking. The showground gates will be open, and yes, there is parking in there? But it's about twenty spaces and every one of them is spoken for by an exhibitor's van.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So what we're asking is that everybody leaves the car at the primary school and walks up the footpath. It's four minutes. And no, the main street is not shut all weekend, whatever you may have read. It's closed to cars on the Sunday morning only, for the parade.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And what's new. People keep asking whether we're going to three days. There's talk of it, there has been talk of it for years, and it is not happening this year. The genuinely new thing is that the dates have shifted onto the public holiday, which is why the caravan park is already full.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's me done. Program's on the back of your ticket, the uni students in the green shirts know more than I do, and if it rains, everything moves into the pavilion and we all get to know each other rather well.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt: The event began as a project run by students in ______.
questions.explanation: 'Students in' predicts a school year, so a number was coming. She says the wrong year first and corrects herself inside the same breath, then repeats the right one. The last value stated before she moves on is the answer, and she gives it twice.

questions.prompt: Last year the weekend was attended by about ______ people.
questions.explanation: 'About' plus 'people' predicts a rounded figure, so expect thousands at a town event. She gives the number they promised the council first and frames it as a forecast. 'Last year we counted' is the switch to what actually happened.

questions.prompt: The only part of the program that visitors pay for is the ______.
questions.explanation: 'Only part' plus 'pay for' predicts a single thing with a price attached, so the price itself is not the answer. 'Almost none of it costs you anything' sets the frame and the exception follows immediately. One word, and the price after it is a decoy for careless pens.

questions.prompt: Every volunteer needs to collect a ______ from the front desk.
questions.explanation: 'A' before the gap predicts a singular countable object. She offers the vests first and cancels them with 'nobody wore them, so we've stopped'. 'What every volunteer does need' is the endorsement, and one word follows it.

questions.prompt: an activity for children who are not yet at school
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the near-miss venue to be named in the same breath. She raises the pavilion's colouring table first and says people mistake it for this. 'The actual little kids' program' is the endorsement, and it is at the school.

questions.prompt: a session that cannot begin until it is dark
questions.explanation: The stem never says astronomy and she never says dark-dependent, so match on the reason. 'That one can't start until it's properly dark' is the signpost, and the venue arrives as the only unlit flat space in town. The word telescope is your bridge from the opening.

questions.prompt: an activity moved because of the noise it makes
questions.explanation: The stem predicts a move, so listen for a past location and a present one. 'Used to be behind the school' plus 'several conversations with the neighbours' is the whole story in one line, and 'this year' switches to the current venue.

questions.prompt: the only session that has to be booked in advance
questions.explanation: 'Only' and 'booked' predict a capacity limit somewhere. She gives the room, then the number twice, then the consequence. The booking rule is stated after the venue, so a learner waiting for the word 'book' must hold the venue in mind for a whole clause.

questions.prompt: What does Alison ask visitors to do about parking?
questions.explanation: The stem asks what she asks, so predict an instruction and expect a concession first. She admits there is parking at the showground and then removes it in the same sentence. 'What we're asking is' is the endorsement, and the closure of the street is limited to one morning.

questions.prompt: What is new about this year's Science Weekend?
questions.explanation: 'New' predicts a contrast with previous years, so expect old things to be named as old. She kills the three-day idea as talk and the teachers' session was mentioned earlier as an annual fixture. 'The genuinely new thing is' leaves only one candidate standing.

parts.title: Tutorial: planning a canteen food-waste project

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Robyn and Dev, discussing a food waste project with their tutor, Doctor Ashfield. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Come in, both of you. Right, the food waste proposal. I've read it twice, and I want to start with something you've tucked away at the bottom of page two.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The bit about the kitchen.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The bit about the kitchen. You've written, and I'm quoting you here, we hope to have access to the kitchen. Hope isn't a research design. Has anybody actually said yes?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Um, sort of. I emailed the catering office. Well, the general address. Which I'm now realising is probably not the same thing at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It isn't. Her name's Ferris, she runs the canteen, and she answers her own email within a day. I've put us in for Thursday morning.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Good. Then that's the first thing that happens, before you buy a single set of scales. Everything else in this proposal is guesswork until she's said yes in writing.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fine. So the plan is, we weigh what comes back on the plates. Every lunchtime, for a fortnight.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And the kitchen?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The kitchen's the same thing, though, isn't it? Food that nobody ate.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It really isn't. What comes back off a plate is a portioning problem. What gets cut off a carrot before service is a purchasing problem. Different causes, different fixes, and if you tip them into one bin you can't tell us anything about either.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we weigh them separately.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's two sets of scales, though. And I'd rather we did the plates properly than did both of them badly.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Mm. That's a fair worry, and I did wonder about telling you to drop the kitchen side altogether. But you've got four weeks, and Ferris will lend you her own scales. So, no.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Both, then.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Both, weighed separately, and that's the version I want to see on Monday.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Now. You originally pitched me a supermarket study. What happened to that?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: They said no. Well, not exactly no. The manager was quite keen, actually, but then head office wanted a form signed by somebody who doesn't even work in the building.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And it would have been six weeks of waiting for that signature. We've got four weeks in total.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Which is the right call, and I want it in your write-up. A project that dies on paperwork is a finding about the sector, not a failure on your part.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Can I ask about the questionnaire?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Go on.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's twelve questions at the moment. We wanted to ask people what they think about food waste generally.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And they'll all tell you it's terrible, and then scrape half a plate into the bin. Everybody's opinion on waste is excellent. Their behaviour isn't. Ask them what they had, how hungry they were when they queued, and whether they finished it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: When do we hand it out? While they're queuing?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Catch them on the way to the bins, when they can see what they've left. In the queue they're guessing.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: So less attitude, more what actually happened.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: More what actually happened, and four questions maximum. That's the questionnaire I'll sign off.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One more thing. Dev wants photographs of the trays coming back.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: For the poster, mainly. I'm not counting anything off them.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Then take them. But you don't need ethics approval to weigh a bin, and you do need it the moment a photograph could identify somebody. A tray with a phone sitting on it identifies somebody. Get the form in this week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: This week. Understood.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. You've got a list at the back of things you'd like to add if there's time. Let's go through them, because some of them are free and some of them are a whole term's work.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First one's the delivery records. What the kitchen orders in, week by week.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Ferris keeps those on a spreadsheet and she'll email them to you on Thursday. Take them. That's one afternoon of your life and it doubles the size of your data set.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then interviews with the serving staff. They watch what comes back all day, every day.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: They do, and it's the most interesting thing on your list. It's also four consent forms, a transcription, and a coding scheme you haven't been taught yet. Not in four weeks.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Not this time, then.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Third. A pilot day.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Just to check the scales work and the tray trolley doesn't get emptied before we reach it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Do it. But not the way you've described it, because you've written pilot day as though it's a rehearsal. It isn't. Decide beforehand what would make you change the method, and write that down, or you'll pilot it, find something awkward, and carry on regardless.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fourth. We wondered about running the same fortnight in the halls kitchen, so we'd have a comparison.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Mm. Two sites, half the depth. And the halls kitchen is self-catering, so you'd be setting a canteen against three hundred people cooking for themselves. That isn't a comparison, it's a second project.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Fair enough.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And the last thing on the list, the online survey of the whole department.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That was mine. Two hundred responses instead of forty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It would be two hundred responses about how people feel, and we've just spent twenty minutes agreeing that feelings aren't your data. Although. If you asked one thing, one, how many days a week do you eat here, you'd have a denominator. Do that, and only that, and think hard about the wording.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One question. How many days a week.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Exactly that. Right. Monday, the revised proposal, and Ferris's yes in writing. Off you go.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt: What does Doctor Ashfield say the students must do first?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect all three actions to be named aloud. The tutor's phrase that's the first thing that happens marks the instruction, and she defines it as a yes in writing. The email has already been sent, so it cannot be a next step. Take the endorsed action, not the mentioned one.

questions.prompt: What do they finally decide about the two kinds of waste?
questions.explanation: Predict a settled outcome, because the stem says finally. The tutor floats dropping the kitchen side, then refuses her own suggestion, and the agreed version is stated last and shortest. Single-bin collection is only ever described as the thing that would destroy the data. Take the quiet closing line.

questions.prompt: Why did the students abandon their supermarket study?
questions.explanation: The stem asks why, so predict a reason and expect more than one to be offered. Dev opens with They said no and takes it back in the same breath. The reason that survives is arithmetic: six weeks of waiting against four weeks of project. Take the reason nobody withdraws.

questions.prompt: What does Doctor Ashfield want the questionnaire to focus on?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the printed words to be planted in a wrong option. Dev says the exact phrase in option A one turn early. The tutor's contrast, opinion excellent, behaviour not, announces her preference, and she then lists three questions that are all about the meal in front of you.

questions.prompt: What does Doctor Ashfield say about the photographs?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and predict a negative, because permission questions are usually answered with a not first. She says no approval is needed to weigh a bin, then flips: you do need it the moment a photograph could identify somebody. The mark sits in the second half of one sentence.

questions.prompt: The kitchen's delivery records
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect a cost to be named for every item. Here she names none. Take them is an instruction with no condition attached, and the two reasons that follow are both in favour. This is the calibration item: it tells you what an unqualified yes sounds like in her mouth.

questions.prompt: Interviews with the serving staff
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect praise before a verdict. She calls this the most interesting item on the list, which is the warmest thing she says all tutorial, then prices it in consent forms and training they have not had. Not in four weeks is the verdict, and it is four words long.

questions.prompt: A pilot day before the main study
questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and notice that as planned is doing the work in option A. She says Do it, so the item survives, then spends four clauses on how it has to change. An instruction about how, not whether, is the middle letter every time.

questions.prompt: A parallel study in the halls kitchen
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and listen for the shape of her refusals, which is a cost and then a sentence beginning That isn't. Two sites, half the depth is the cost; the self-catering point is the evidence; a second project is the verdict. No condition is offered, so no rewrite is on the table.

questions.prompt: An online survey of the whole department
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the reversal this set has been building to. She argues against it for two clauses, says Although as a whole sentence, and then licenses one question only, with a warning about the wording. Approval plus a condition is never the plain go-ahead letter.

parts.title: Lecture: peat bogs and the carbon they hold

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about peat bogs and the carbon they hold. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Morning, everyone. Last week we finished with woodland soils, and today I want to go to the other end of the scale — to ground that looks like nothing at all and holds an extraordinary amount of carbon. Peat. I'll take the formation first, then what's gone wrong, and then the repair work.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, formation. Peat is just plant material that has died and then failed to rot. And the reason it fails to rot is water. Where the rain coming in is greater than what the ground can drain away, the soil stays waterlogged, and waterlogged ground has almost no oxygen in it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And once the oxygen's gone, the bacteria that would normally break everything down simply can't work. So the material piles up instead. Very slowly, mind you — a healthy bog puts on well under a millimetre a year.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, one plant does most of this work, and it's worth having the name because everything else follows from it. The moss is sphagnum. I'll spell that: S. P. H. A. G. N. U. M. It holds many times its own weight in water, and it turns the ground around it acid.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Keep that going for a few thousand years and the peat builds into a dome that sits above the surrounding water table. When it does that, we call it a raised bog, and a raised bog is fed by nothing but rainfall. No groundwater at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Before I leave the formation, a quick aside, because somebody always asks. Peat preserves things. Leather, wooden trackways, the occasional unfortunate traveller. There's a bronze-age walkway on the Norland moors that came out of the ground in one piece. It's the reason bog archaeology exists as a field.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Anyway. Back to the carbon, because that's the reason any of this is on your reading list.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right — the damage. And almost all of it starts the same way. Somebody cuts ditches across the moor to drain it, so that the ground will carry sheep, or trees, or both. And the ditches work. That's the trouble. They work beautifully.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Once the water table drops, peat meets air for the first time in millennia and it starts to oxidise. The surface sinks. Across the Norland survey the average was around two centimetres a year. Sorry, no — two is the gentle end. On the worst of the drained sites, make that five.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And there's a second loss that people underestimate, and it is fire. Dried peat will burn underground, sometimes for months on end. And no, it isn't the grazing that finishes a drained site off, whatever you read in the papers. It's the fire.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So that's the mechanism. Now the findings, and this is the part that changed the policy.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The Norland team measured gas exchange on twelve moors for four years, drained and undrained side by side. And the headline is simple enough. A healthy bog takes in a little more carbon than it gives off. A drained one gives off far more than it takes in. It has flipped from being a store to being a source.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The other number worth writing down is what happens when the water goes back. Rewetting doesn't restore the bog — that takes centuries — but on those sites it cut the annual carbon loss by around seventy per cent within three years.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Repair. And the good news is that the cheapest technique is also the best one, which almost never happens in this subject.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You block the ditches. Somebody walks the line with a digger and puts a dam in every few metres, and the dams are made of peat — cut from beside the ditch, dropped in, trodden down. No concrete, no plastic, nothing imported at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the thing that stops it isn't the digger and it isn't the money. A scheme on this scale costs less than resurfacing a mile of road. What stops it, every time, is ownership. One moor can have eleven or twelve owners with different ideas, and you need every one of them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, three things to take away. Water is what makes the store, the ditch is what breaks it, and the obstacle at the end is a legal one and not a technical one. Next week, saltmarsh, which does the same job faster and is even less popular.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt:
PEAT AND CARBON
Formation
- Dead plants fail to rot because waterlogged ground contains almost no ______.
questions.explanation: Predict an uncountable noun, something ground can contain. 'The reason it fails to rot is' announces the cause. She says waterlogged ground has almost no oxygen in it. No decoy here. One word, and no article in front of it.

questions.prompt: - Most of the peat is built by a moss called ______.
questions.explanation: 'A moss called' tells you before the audio that this is a name you cannot guess, so it will be spelled. 'I'll spell that' is the cue to stop listening for meaning and take single letters. Eight letters, p-h at the front and g-n in the middle.

questions.prompt: - Peat that has grown above the water table forms a ______ bog, fed only by rain.
questions.explanation: A printed noun after the gap, so predict a describing word. 'We call it' is the definition marker and in this paper the defined term is usually the answer. She says a raised bog, fed by nothing but rainfall. One word, past-participle form.

questions.prompt:
Damage
- Damage nearly always starts when ditches are cut across a moor in order to ______ it.
questions.explanation: 'In order to' forces a base-form verb, which rules out every noun you might hear. 'Right — the damage' opens the section. She says somebody cuts ditches across the moor to drain it. Write the bare form, with no -s and no -ing.

questions.prompt: - On the worst drained sites the surface sinks by about ______ centimetres a year.
questions.explanation: The unit is printed, so predict a bare figure in single digits. She gives two centimetres, then corrects herself out loud. 'Sorry, no' means the value is about to change, and the figure attached to 'the worst of the drained sites' is five.

questions.prompt: - The second loss, and the one most often underestimated, is caused by ______.
questions.explanation: 'A second loss' told you a countable list was running, so you were already waiting. She names it in the same clause, then spends two sentences cancelling grazing with one unstressed 'isn't'. Write the noun she endorses, not the one she dismisses.

questions.prompt:
Findings
- A drained bog gives out more carbon than it takes in, so it has become a net ______.
questions.explanation: 'A net' forces a singular noun. 'The headline is simple enough' marks the sentence that matters. The word 'store' arrives first and describes the healthy bog; the drained one has flipped to a source. Take the noun on the far side of 'to'.

questions.prompt: - Rewetting cut the yearly carbon loss by roughly ______ per cent.
questions.explanation: 'Per cent' is printed, so predict a bare figure that could be a percentage. She announces it as a number worth writing down. Two figures land in one clause, seventy and three, and only the one attached to 'per cent' answers the printed frame.

questions.prompt:
Repair
- The ditches are blocked with small dams built from ______.
questions.explanation: 'Built from' wants a material, and materials are uncountable. 'You block the ditches' opens the technique in five words. She says the dams are made of peat, cut from beside the ditch. The word is the subject of the whole lecture, which is why it feels too easy.

questions.prompt: - The real obstacle to restoration is not cost but ______.
questions.explanation: The printed frame already rules cost out, so predict an abstract noun that is not money. 'What stops it, every time, is' is as loud an emphasis marker as she gives. Money is raised and priced first; the answer arrives afterwards.

parts.title: Signing up for a first-aid course

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a man signing up for a course at the front desk of a community recreation center in the United States. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hi there. Are you signing up for a class, or just picking up a schedule?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Signing up, I hope. My employer wants me certified before the fall, and somebody at work said you run the course here. I've left it late, I know, but they only told me on Friday.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We do, twice a year. Let me pull up the sign-up sheet. Can I get a last name?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Vasquez.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: How do you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: V. A. S. Q. U. E. Z. Vasquez.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Let me read that back to you. V. A. S. Q. U. E. S.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's a Z on the end, not an S. Everybody does that, don't worry.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Z. Sorry about that, I've fixed it. And a cell number?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Sure. Two one four, five five five, oh nine eight three.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Two one four, five five five, oh nine eight three. Perfect.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, we run two courses this session, and people mix them up all the time. There's water safety, which is mostly pool work, and there's first aid. Same room, same instructor, completely different certificate at the end.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The water safety one. Um, no, hold on, sorry. It's first aid I need. The certificate my employer asked for is the first aid one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First aid it is. That's the Level 2 certificate, and it's the one most employers around here ask for.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That sounds right. Which night is it?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First aid meets Wednesdays. Six weeks, seven until nine thirty, in the room on the first floor at the end of the hall.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Wednesdays are good for me. And when does the whole thing start?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: September. We were going to open on the ninth, but half the town is away that holiday weekend, so we pushed it back to the sixteenth.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The sixteenth. Okay, I can make that work.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Great. The fee is sixty dollars, and we do take it at sign-up rather than on the first night. That covers all six weeks and the assessment at the end.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Can I put it on a card?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You could last month. The card reader has been down since Thursday and nobody can tell me when it's coming back, so today it's cash or a check.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I'll write you a check, then. My checkbook's out in the car, I'll bring it in.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's fine, I'll hold the spot while you go get it. Nobody else is going to take it in the next four minutes.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Okay. A few things about what to bring, because everybody asks me the same four questions. Two of them are about parking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go ahead. I'd rather know now than turn up wrong.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The workbook first. That one's in the price, and there'll be a copy on your chair the first night. Don't buy one online, people do that every session and then they've paid for the thing twice.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Good to know. I nearly did that already.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The pocket mask is a different story. That one you get from us, twelve dollars, and it's yours to keep afterwards. We handed them out free for years, but they walked off faster than we could order them.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the dummies you practice on? Do I need my own?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The manikins are ours. You'll each have one for the whole session, at no charge, and they go back in the crate at the end of every night. Same with the training defibrillators.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's a relief. What about parking? I picked up a ticket in that lot last spring.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You'll want a lot pass, and that's not something we hand out with the course. You buy one at the front desk, five dollars.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It sticks inside the windshield and it's good for the whole six weeks, so hang on to it. People bring me the old one back in the spring, which I promise you I do not need.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: So the book is free, the mask and the pass I pay for, and the manikin goes back in the crate.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's exactly it. You've got it in one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh, and wear something you can kneel in. Half of this course happens on the floor, and good pants do not survive it. Sneakers, not sandals.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Noted. Thanks for your help.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Any time. Go get that checkbook and I'll print your receipt.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
