parts.title: A guided tour of Brackenfield Watermill

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a volunteer guide showing a group of visitors round a restored watermill on a Saturday morning. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, morning everybody, and welcome to Brackenfield. I'm Ellen, I've been a volunteer here since the wheel went back in, and I'll be taking you round. Do grab a plan off the pile by the gate, because the site is a great deal more spread out than it looks from the lane.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So. We're all standing just inside the entrance, and the entrance is the thing I want you to hold on to. Turn so the gate's behind you and the mill building is over on your left. Every left and every right I give you from now on is from exactly where you're standing.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Straight away on your left, tucked in against the near end of the mill, is the sack store. Little stone shed, tin roof. That's where the grain came in off the carts, and it's where we keep the wheelbarrows now, so it's rather less romantic than it sounds.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, directly opposite that, across the cobbles, you'll see the old hand pump. The pump isn't marked on your plan at all, so please don't go writing anything in for it. What is marked, immediately behind it, is the tea room. Scones, and a queue, from about eleven.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Carry on up the yard with the stream on your right. A few yards short of the footbridge you'll see a set of black timber boards standing in the water. That's the sluice gate. That's what lets water into the wheel, and one of us opens it at ten every morning.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now cross the footbridge. Over on the far bank you've got a long thin strip of reed bed.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No, sorry, that's wrong. The reed bed is away downstream by the weir. What's over there, on your right as you come off the bridge, is the willow beds. We cut those every winter and they go off to a basket maker in the village.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then double back over the bridge, and right at the top of the yard, behind the mill, is the orchard. One or two of the older leaflets still call that corner the cider yard, and it was the cider yard, until the restoration. It's the orchard now, and the apples are yours if you can reach them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So that's the ground covered. I'll take questions on any of it at the end. Let's get on, because the wheel starts turning at half past and you'll want to be standing inside the mill when it does.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the tour, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. How the thing actually works, because this is the bit almost everybody gets wrong. The wheel is not sitting in the river. The river is two fields away. The water comes to us along a channel that was dug in the sixteen hundreds, and that channel has a name. It's called the leat. L. E. A. T.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It runs behind the hedge you walked in past, and it drops by about a foot over the length of the site, which doesn't sound like anything at all. But the drop is what does the work. No drop, no flour.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, when can you see it working. Everybody assumes we grind every day of the week. We don't, and we can't, because the stones would be worn down inside a year. The stones turn on Saturday afternoons, from two o'clock, and only then.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then there's the shop, which is inside the tea room, confusingly, and which is staffed entirely by people my age who will talk to you for as long as you let them. We sell what we grind. Wholemeal, and a coarser stoneground that is very good and very slow to cook.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Prices. The small bags, the half-kilo ones, are two pounds. The big bags, and the big bags are the ones you actually want because they freeze beautifully, the big bags are five pounds.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Access now, and I'm sorry about this one. The whole of the ground floor is level, and there's a ramp at the side door, so the wheel and the stones are fine for everybody. Apart from one place. It's the bin floor, right up at the top, that we cannot get anyone to.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And while I think of it, the bin floor is called the bin floor because the grain sat in bins up there and came down by gravity. Everything in a mill comes down by gravity. That is the entire idea of the building, and it's why it's tall and thin.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Last thing and then I'll shut up. We are all volunteers here, and we are short of people. If you have ever thought about it, what we ask is two days a month. Not two days a week, which is what people hear, and then they go pale. Two a month. We'll teach you the rest.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. The wheel goes on in about four minutes. If you want to be underneath it when it starts, and you do, follow me round the side. Mind the step there, it's the wettest thing on this site.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.explanation: Predict a two-word building name on the left of the path. 'Straight away on your left' announces it, and she puts the sack store against the near end of the mill. Nothing competes with it. Two words only, so leave the article off.

Predict something facing 11 across the yard. She names the hand pump first and then says outright that it is not on your plan. The label is what sits behind it. A place named to steer you is never the answer; wait for 'what is marked'.

Predict something on the water side, before the printed footbridge. 'A few yards short of the footbridge' fixes it against a landmark already drawn on your plan, so you can place it before you know the word. She then describes it and names it. Two words.

Predict the first position over the water. She starts to say reed bed, stops herself in the next breath and says the reed bed is somewhere else entirely. The answer is the value she leaves standing. Plural: she cuts them, and the plan draws a strip.

Only the far end is left, so predict the top of the plan. 'Right at the top of the yard, behind the mill' places it, and she names it first. Then she gives the corner's old name and marks it as old with 'it was, until the restoration'. Write the present-tense one.

questions.prompt:
BRACKENFIELD WATERMILL — VISITOR NOTES
How it works
- The channel that carries water to the wheel is called the ______.
questions.explanation: 'Is called the' is a definition frame, so predict a term you may not know. 'That channel has a name' is the cue, and she spells the word out immediately afterwards. No competing value. Copy the four letters as she gives them, not as you would guess them.

questions.prompt: - Grinding takes place on ______ afternoons only.
questions.explanation: 'Afternoons' in the printed line tells you a day is coming, so predict a weekday before she opens her mouth. She kills the everyday assumption first, then states the day plainly. Write the day only: 'afternoons' is already printed and repeating it puts you over the limit.

questions.prompt:
The shop
- A large bag of flour costs ______ pounds.
questions.explanation: 'Pounds' is printed, so predict a bare figure in single digits. She gives the small bags first, then talks up the big ones, then gives their price. Two prices in one breath and only one printed frame: 'large' is the word that decides it.

questions.prompt:
Access
- Wheelchair users can reach everything except the ______ floor.
questions.explanation: The printed 'floor' fixes the slot: one word naming a level. She spends a whole sentence saying what is accessible, and 'apart from one place' flips it. The ground floor is the value she gives first and it is the one the frame excludes.

questions.prompt:
Volunteering
- New volunteers are asked to give ______ days a month.
questions.explanation: 'Days a month' is printed, so predict a small figure and expect a rival unit. 'What we ask is' marks the commitment. She then names the figure people mishear, and names the unit they mishear it as. The month version is the one attached to the ask.

parts.title: Tutorial feedback: a report on remote call-centre work

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Jodie and Trent, discussing a draft report with their professor, Professor Linden. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: OK, come on in. So, this is the draft on remote work at the call center, and I'd rather be useful than polite, so I'll start with the thing that costs you the most points.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The conclusion.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: No, actually, the conclusion is the best page in here. It's the research question. You've asked whether remote work improved performance, and then you've measured four different things and called all of them performance.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Handle time and resolution rate, yeah.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Plus absence. And turnover.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Two of those are performance. Two of them are retention. They can move in opposite directions, and in your own data they do. So the question has to name which one you're testing, or the report spends nine pages arguing with itself.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we pick one.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You pick one, and you say why. Let's be specific. Which one does the company actually care about?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Turnover. They said so in the first meeting. They lose about a third of the floor every year, and it costs a fortune to train replacements.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Then that's your question, and everything else in here becomes context. Three sentences of rewriting, and this is a much better report.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Can I ask about the literature section? I put in eleven sources and it still felt thin.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It is thin, but not because eleven isn't enough. It's thin because nine of them agree with you.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Isn't that good?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It's comfortable. There's a whole literature saying remote work makes call centers worse, and you've cited one paper from it, in a footnote, and moved on. Half of what you do cite is about office teams anyway. Bring that argument into the body and answer it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Hold on. If we bring in the counter-argument, doesn't that weaken our own conclusion?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The opposite. An argument that has never met an objection isn't an argument, it's a preference. And your grader has read that literature.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. And the referencing? I think I mixed two versions of the department style.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You did, and it's the one thing in here the rubric marks mechanically. Pick the version on the syllabus and be boring about it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Could we ask for an extension?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You could, and I'd probably give you one, but then you'd be revising in the middle of your other finals.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The department deadline is the twenty-eighth. Don't aim for that. Aim for the Friday before, because the writing center is booked solid for the last three days of every semester.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. The raw material. You've listed six things at the back of the draft. Let's take them in the order you've got them, because two of them have a problem.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The turnover file first. Human resources sent it over as a spreadsheet.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That one's your spine. It goes back five years, it's already anonymized, and I'd build the whole results section around it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then the exit interviews. Those are pretty personal.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Those are fine, actually. Human resources ran them, everybody signed a consent form at the time, and the names came off before you ever saw them. Use them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And Marcus's notes? He's the team leader on nights, and he wrote down what people told him about working from home.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And did any of those people know they were being written down? No. So the team leader's notes stay in your drawer until Marcus goes back and asks them.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then the shift logs. About four hundred rows of clock-in times.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Four hundred rows isn't a finding, it's an exhibit. One summary table in the body, and the rows themselves go at the back where nobody has to read them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The customer survey's ours. We ran it in March.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You did, and it's the freshest thing in the pile. Two pages of it in the body, please, not eleven.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the benchmark report? The industry one, with the sector averages.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Which edition?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The one on the association's website.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That edition is six years old, and the whole sector changed after it came out. Cite it if you want a before picture, but you can't use it as your comparison, because it describes a world that stopped existing.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Two more things. Trent, in your email you said you'd redo the graphs.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I said tables. The graphs are Jodie's.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The graphs are mine, and honestly they're the bit I'm least sure about.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Then start with them. Every graph in here needs a caption that says what the reader is supposed to notice, not just what the axes are.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And when do we see you again?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Come to office hours on Tuesday, both of you, and bring the rewritten question on one sheet of paper. Not the whole draft. One sheet.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: One sheet. Got it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Good. And Trent, the tables. Tuesday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt: What does Professor Linden say is the main weakness of the draft?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the students to guess first. Jodie offers the conclusion; the professor says no and names the research question instead. Four things measured and all four called performance is what too broad means here. The opposite-directions point is the symptom she then describes, not the weakness she names.

questions.prompt: What do they agree the report should measure?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and note that all four candidate measures are read out early, so option spotting is worthless. Her question, which one does the company care about, is the signpost. Trent answers with the company's own reason: a third of the floor gone every year. Clean item, and it rewards waiting for the reason.

questions.prompt: What is Professor Linden's criticism of the literature section?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and watch the ownership of the complaint. Jodie says the section felt thin, which is her diagnosis, not the professor's. The professor keeps the word thin and changes the cause: nine of eleven agree with you. The office-teams point is a second remark, made in passing.

questions.prompt: Why does Professor Linden want the counter-argument in the report?
questions.explanation: The stem asks why, so predict a reason, and Trent has just supplied the wrong one by asking whether it weakens the conclusion. Her single word Opposite is the whole answer, and the sentence after it explains the mechanism. Reading widely is a side benefit she mentions last, about the grader, not about the argument.

questions.prompt: What does Professor Linden advise about handing the report in?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect two dates, because deadline advice always names the official one first. She gives the twenty-eighth, cancels it in three words, and names the Friday before. The extension she offers and then talks them out of, and the writing center is her reason, not her advice.

questions.prompt: It cannot be used until the people in it have been asked.
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect consent to be raised about the wrong source first. Trent flags the exit interviews as personal and the professor clears them. The notes fail on one test only: nobody in them knew they were being recorded. Her rhetorical question is the signal, and the verdict follows it in one clause.

questions.prompt: It belongs in an appendix rather than in the body of the report.
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and listen for the word back, which is her shorthand for an appendix. Four hundred rows is an exhibit is the judgement, and the instruction splits the source in two: a summary table in the body, the rows at the back. Only one source gets that treatment.

questions.prompt: It no longer describes the industry accurately.
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect an age word. Her question, which edition, is the signpost, and six years old is the finding. Then she half-licenses it: cite it as a before picture. That permission is the trap, because it is permission to do something the stem is not asking about.

questions.prompt: Every graph in the report needs a ______ explaining what the reader should notice.
questions.explanation: Predict a singular noun, because the printed a fixes it. Then start with them announces the instruction, and the word arrives three words later. She defines it in the same breath, which is how you spell it: a line under a graph telling the reader what to see. One word, no plural.

questions.prompt: On Tuesday the students will bring one sheet of paper to Professor Linden's ______.
questions.explanation: Predict a place or a time slot, because a possessive stands in front of the gap. Jodie's question is the cue, and the answer is the first thing in the reply. Tuesday and one sheet are both printed already, so anything you write beyond the two words is over the limit.

parts.title: Lecture: putting nutrients into everyday food

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about adding nutrients to everyday food. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. Good morning. Today we're on fortification, which is the practice of putting a nutrient into a food that people are already eating anyway. I want to do three things: define it properly, walk you through the two big programs, and then explain why the hard part of this work has almost nothing to do with chemistry.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, definition first. Fortification is not supplementation. A supplement is a pill, and a pill needs somebody to remember it every single day, forever. Fortification puts the nutrient into something that's already in the kitchen. And the food you pick to carry it — we call that food the vehicle.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Choosing the vehicle is most of the job, and it's harder than it sounds. It has to be something nearly everybody buys, in roughly the same amount, whether they're wealthy or poor, in the city or way out in the country. That rules out an enormous amount of the grocery store straight away.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The working rule is that a vehicle has to reach at least sixty per cent of households before the program is worth running. Sorry — sixty was the old figure, from the early days. The threshold most agencies use now is ninety.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which brings me to the one food that clears that bar everywhere. The first vehicle anybody used, and still the most successful one, was salt. Everybody buys salt. A wealthy household and a poor household buy almost exactly the same quantity of it, and that is very nearly unique.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And what iodized salt prevents is a swelling at the base of the neck. The gland is the thyroid — I'll spell it, because it's all over the reading: T. H. Y. R. O. I. D. Starve it of iodine and it grows, sometimes enormously.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, one aside, and then I'll get back to the programs. The salt producers fought this for years, and not on health grounds. On taste. There were blind tastings, there were letters to the newspapers, and it turned out nobody could tell the difference. A nice little story about how a technical fix becomes a political fight.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Anyway. The second program, and the more recent one, is folic acid. And here the vehicle is not salt, it's flour, because the mills add it before the grain ever leaves the site.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The timing is the whole point of that one. Folic acid protects the neural tube, and the neural tube closes inside the first month — often before anybody knows there's a pregnancy at all. Which is exactly why a pill can't do this job and a loaf of bread can. You don't have to know, and you don't have to comply.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the hard part. It isn't the chemistry. The chemistry was settled decades ago and it hasn't moved since. What's hard is the monitoring. You have to know how much is actually in the sack at the far end of a supply chain, and in most places nobody measures it twice.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right — the table on your handout. Three nutrients, and one characteristic problem each.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Iodine first. Salt is cheap and it's everywhere, but iodine is volatile. Leave a sack out on a loading dock and you lose a good part of it. So the problem in the iodine row is sunlight, and the fix is nothing cleverer than opaque packaging.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Folic acid next. Students often write birth weight in that box, and birth weight is a genuine finding, but it belongs to a completely different program. The aim in the flour row is early pregnancy, and it's early pregnancy that goes in that cell.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Vitamin D. Different vehicle again. This one goes into milk, and in some countries into breakfast cereal as well, but milk is the standard and milk is what your table wants. It works because the fat carries it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the problem in that row is dose. It's set by law in most places, yes, but the enforcement is loose, and if you test cartons off the shelf the amount varies by brand — sometimes by a factor of three.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, to close. The nutrient is the easy part of a fortification program. The vehicle decides whether it reaches anybody at all, and the measuring decides whether it stays honest once the news coverage has moved on. Next week we'll look at what happens when a government quietly stops funding the testing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt:
FORTIFYING FOOD
Definition
- The everyday food chosen to carry a nutrient is called the ______.
questions.explanation: 'Is called the' promises a term, so predict a singular noun you may not know. 'We call that food' is the definition marker, and in a lecture the defined word is very often the answer. She says the vehicle. One word, no article.

questions.prompt: - A usable vehicle must now reach at least ______ per cent of households.
questions.explanation: The word 'now' in the printed frame is doing real work: it warns you that an older figure exists. She gives sixty, says sorry, and calls sixty the old number. The current threshold is ninety. Bare figure only.

questions.prompt:
Iodine
- The first vehicle used, and still the most successful, was ______.
questions.explanation: The heading already says iodine, so predict a food. 'The first vehicle anybody used' repeats the printed frame almost word for word, which is your warning that the answer lands in the same clause. Clean item, one word, no article.

questions.prompt: - Without iodine, the ______ gland in the neck swells.
questions.explanation: A printed noun follows the gap, so predict the word in front of it, not another noun. 'I'll spell it' is your instruction to stop listening for meaning. Seven letters, and the y in the second position is the one people lose.

questions.prompt:
Folic acid
- The vehicle is ______, treated at the mill before the grain leaves.
questions.explanation: New heading, so predict a second food. She names the wrong one first, inside a negative: 'the vehicle is not salt, it's flour'. Take the noun after the comma. One word, and mind the homophone in your own writing.

questions.prompt:
Difficulty
- The hard part of any program is not the chemistry but the ______.
questions.explanation: The frame rules chemistry out before she speaks, so predict a different abstract noun. 'So, the hard part' opens the section and she repeats the printed structure exactly. She names measuring the sack at the far end. Write the -ing noun.

questions.prompt:
| Nutrient | Vehicle | Aim | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|
| Iodine | salt | prevent swelling of the thyroid | lost if stored in **37** ______ |
| Folic acid | flour | protect early **38** ______ | reaches only industrial bakeries |
| Vitamin D | **39** ______ | bone strength | dose varies by **40** ______ |
questions.explanation: 'Stored in' wants a condition, not a container, so predict weather or light rather than a box. She names the row first, then says the problem in the iodine row is sunlight. Clean item, and the fix she names afterwards confirms it.

questions.prompt:
| Nutrient | Vehicle | Aim | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|
| Iodine | salt | prevent swelling of the thyroid | lost if stored in **37** ______ |
| Folic acid | flour | protect early **38** ______ | reaches only industrial bakeries |
| Vitamin D | **39** ______ | bone strength | dose varies by **40** ______ |
questions.explanation: 'Protect early' wants a stage, not a measurement. She raises birth weight first, agrees it is real, and then says it belongs to a different programme. The aim in the flour row is early pregnancy. Singular after 'early'.

questions.prompt:
| Nutrient | Vehicle | Aim | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|
| Iodine | salt | prevent swelling of the thyroid | lost if stored in **37** ______ |
| Folic acid | flour | protect early **38** ______ | reaches only industrial bakeries |
| Vitamin D | **39** ______ | bone strength | dose varies by **40** ______ |
questions.explanation: The column is Vehicle and the other two vehicles are single uncountable foods, so predict a third. 'Different vehicle again' announces it. Breakfast cereal is offered as a second option in some countries; she says milk is the standard.

questions.prompt:
| Nutrient | Vehicle | Aim | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|
| Iodine | salt | prevent swelling of the thyroid | lost if stored in **37** ______ |
| Folic acid | flour | protect early **38** ______ | reaches only industrial bakeries |
| Vitamin D | **39** ______ | bone strength | dose varies by **40** ______ |
questions.explanation: 'Varies by' wants the thing that differs from carton to carton, so predict a singular countable noun. She concedes the dose is set by law, then flips it with 'but the enforcement is loose'. The mark is on the second clause: it varies by brand.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man joining a bushwalking club in Australia and the club's secretary. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Talgarra Bushwalking Club, Bronwyn speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: G'day. I'm after joining, if you're still taking people. A bloke at work reckons your Sunday walks are the best thing going.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We are, yeah, we're always after new walkers. I'll take your details and get you on the list. What's the surname?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Halloran.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: How do you spell it?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: H. A. L. O. R. A. N. Ah, no, hang on, there's two L's in it. H. A. double L. O. R. A. N. Halloran.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Two L's. Halloran. Got you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the best mobile for you?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh four one two, double six, three nine, four one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh four one two, double six, three nine, four one. Beautiful.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, membership. There's a family one, which is ninety dollars and covers everyone under your roof. There's a single. And if you're a student or you've got a seniors card, there's a concession rate.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's just me, no kids, no partner. And I'm at uni two days a week, if that counts for anything.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It counts, so you'd be on the concession, not the single. Cheaper, and it's exactly the same walks.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, so I'll put you down for the Sunday group?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Sunday suits me. When's the next one?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first one you can come on is the eighth of March. No, hang on, sorry, the eighth is the long weekend and we never run on public holidays. Make that the fifteenth.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The fifteenth. I'll put it in the phone while we're talking.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Do that. Now, where we meet. It used to be the pub car park out on the highway, and half the old members still turn up there, poor things. We shifted it two years ago.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We meet at the showground car park now, the gravel one round behind the pavilion. Seven o'clock sharp, and I'll be honest, we do leave without people.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Showground. Righto, I'll be early.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the fee. It's fifty-five dollars for the year on a single. The concession one is forty.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Forty. Can I pay that on the day?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You can, or you can do a bank transfer when the newsletter comes out. Either's fine by me.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Righto, that's you on the list. I'll flag you as a first-timer so somebody walks with you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, a few things about the walks themselves, because people turn up unprepared and it makes for a long day.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go on, I'd rather hear it now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Water. Two litres minimum, and I don't care how heavy it feels in the car park. There's no tap once you're through the gate. People bring an esky with sandwiches in it and forget the water completely, and then I'm sharing mine.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Two litres. Right.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Poles are a personal thing. Half the club swears by them and the other half reckons they're a nuisance on rock. Bring them if you already use them, but don't go buying a pair on our account.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: How do I know whether a walk's too hard for me?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Every walk's got a grade, one to five, and it's in the newsletter that goes out on the Thursday. Don't go off the distance, that's the mistake everyone makes. Six kilometres up a ridge will hurt you far more than fifteen on the flat.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's useful. So grade first, distance second.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if you're still not sure, ring the leader. Her number's on the newsletter as well. Mind you, half of them are out of range by the Saturday arvo, so don't leave it late.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And what happens if the weather turns?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We walk in rain, that's just bushwalking. We don't walk on a total fire ban, and we don't walk if the leader calls it off, which she'll do by text the night before. Don't ring the club on the morning, there's nobody in the office on a Sunday.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Text the night before. Got it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Last thing, and this one actually matters. If you've put your name down and then you can't come, tell the leader. We count heads at the car park and we don't move until the numbers add up. One no-show held twenty of us there for forty minutes in January.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Fair enough. Do I get the money back if I miss one?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No refunds, I'm afraid. It's an annual fee, not a per-walk thing.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And no, we don't hand your spot to somebody else either. We're not running a bus service. It's purely the head count at the start.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Understood. I'll text her if anything comes up.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Beauty. See you on the fifteenth, then. Bring the water.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Radio feature: reopening the Norland canal arm

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a local radio presenter introducing a feature about a canal restoration project. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now. If you walk out past the retail park and you take the little gravel track behind the recycling depot, you come to something most people in this town have no idea is there. Half a mile of canal, full of water, and going absolutely nowhere. No boats, no towpath signs, nothing.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Everybody assumes a canal means coal. It usually did. Not this one. The Norland arm was cut to bring limestone down off the hills to the kilns at the basin, and coal only ever came back up it, as a return load, on the empty boats.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The plan, when the trust started, was ambitious. Six miles, all the way to the junction, and there's still a drawing on the wall of their hut to prove it. What they have settled on, and what they are actually digging, is three miles.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: If you want to help, they run work parties. Second Sunday of the month — no, hang on, that's out of date, they shifted it last autumn. It's the first Sunday now. First Sunday, nine till three, and they feed you at one, which I'm told is the real reason people come.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The single biggest obstacle is half a mile up from the basin, where the arm runs under the Ashfield road. There's a culvert there. That's just a pipe carrying the water underneath the road, and it fell in some time in the eighties. Digging that out is a two-year job on its own.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So I asked Sheila Vance, who chairs the trust, what the hold-up really is. I'd assumed money. Everybody assumes money, and the council officer I spoke to talked about funding for a solid twenty minutes. Sheila didn't. She said what they cannot find is bricklayers.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the history and the hole in the ground. What I want to give you now is the practical half, because the trust has three things in the diary and every one of them is open to anybody.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the feature, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, three things in the diary. And I should say that none of these needs you to know the first thing about canals, which is just as well, because a fortnight ago I could not have told you what a lock was for, and I grew up two streets from this one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The open day. That is in September, and it is the one day in the year they put boats back on the water. Trips run from the wharf all afternoon, there's a brass band that has seen better decades, and there is, inevitably, a cake stall.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Winter talks, Thursday evenings from October. They used to be in the community centre and honestly half the town could never find it. They're in the boathouse now, which is warmer, holds forty, and has a kettle that works.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And membership. It's twelve pounds a year for one person, or twenty for a whole household, and it gets you the newsletter and a vote at the annual meeting, which is a livelier evening than you would ever imagine.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then there's the tunnel. Everybody asks about the tunnel. It was surveyed four years ago, properly, with divers and cameras and a very expensive week, and the brickwork turned out to be sound, which nobody had expected.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So it's not that the tunnel's dangerous. It isn't. It's simply that it sits beyond the second lock, and the second lock is not in this phase of the work at all. The tunnel is not part of what is being restored now, whatever you may have read.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, if this is your sort of thing. You can send them money, and they will take it very gratefully indeed. But when I asked Sheila what she actually wanted, it wasn't cheques. It was people standing in a wet ditch on a Sunday with a spade. Turn up to a work party. That is the answer.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The Norland Canal Trust, then. First Sunday of the month, open day in September, and a website address I am not going to attempt to read out on air, because it has a hyphen in it and we would all regret it. It's on our page instead. That's me. Back to the studio.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Choosing a method for a campus cycling study

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Tegan and Hamish, discussing research methods for a cycling study with their supervisor, Doctor Brennan. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Righto, come in, both of you. So, the cycling project. You've got four possible methods on this sheet and about seven weeks, so we're going to lose some of them this morning.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Five, actually. I added the app one on the tram this morning?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Five. Even better. Start me off with the survey, because that's the one you've already drafted.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Online. We'd push it out through the faculty mailing lists, and put a poster up in the bike cage.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And how many responses would you need before it told you anything at all?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Two hundred. We'd probably get four hundred, because everyone on this campus has an opinion about the bike cage.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Then that's your backbone. Everything else you do this semester hangs off it, and it's the only one of the five that gets you numbers you can put in a table.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the interviews? I wanted to sit down with people who've stopped riding.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: So did I, at your age. How long is each one?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Forty minutes? Maybe an hour once you've transcribed it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: An hour each, twenty people, and there goes your whole mid-semester break. Do six.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Six isn't a sample.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Six isn't a sample, no. Six is where your quotes come from, and your quotes are what make the survey numbers mean something to a reader. Different job entirely.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fair.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Then the gate counts. There's a sensor on the footpath by the sports centre, and I reckon we could sit there with a clicker on a couple of mornings as well.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Hang on. If there's already a sensor, then somebody already has that number. Ring facilities, ask for last year's, and don't spend a single morning of your life counting bikes by hand.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we drop the counting.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You drop the counting and you keep the number. Those are two different sentences.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Trip diaries next. A fortnight, and everyone writes down every trip they make.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Everyone won't. Ten people will, if you buy them coffee, and ten good fortnights of diaries would be the most interesting thing in your write-up. Ten. Not everyone.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the app? It'd track the routes automatically.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It would, and it'd also track them to their GP, their house and their Friday night. You'd need a separate ethics application for that, and the committee doesn't sit again until week nine.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Week nine's too late.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Week nine is after your data collection finishes. So that one's gone, and I'd say so in your methods chapter. Explaining what you couldn't do is worth marks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. The survey itself. You've got twenty-six questions in this draft, which is about twenty too many, but I want to talk about the first one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Do you ride to uni. Yes or no.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And what do you do with everybody who says no?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Nothing. They're not our population.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: They're exactly your population. Your question is why people stop, so the interesting person is the one who used to ride and doesn't. If your first question sends them to the end of the form, you've thrown the study away.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we make it a frequency? Never, sometimes, used to, still do?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's better, and it's one question doing the work of two.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The sample, though. We're pushing it through the faculty lists, so that's engineering and science mostly.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Which is where most of the bikes are, so I can see why. But your finding will be about engineering students, not about the campus.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We could hand out cards at the tram stop. The Parkes Road one. Sorry, no, not Parkes Road, the other one, by the sports centre. That's where the riders actually come past.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Do that. And print them properly, don't rely on a code they have to scan, because half of them won't stop long enough.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: When should we open it?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Not in week one. Everybody's timetable is still moving in week one and half of them haven't found the bike cage yet.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And not the week before the mid-semester break, because nobody rides in the week before a break. Week four. Two weeks open, then close it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Do we have to tell people we're recording the interviews?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Someone in our tutorial said you have to write your own consent form for every project.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Someone in your tutorial is wrong. Hamish, you did Doctor Mowbray's methods unit last year. She'll have a template, and hers has already been approved. Use that one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And what's the one thing you'd tell us not to do?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Don't start writing your methods chapter at the end. Write it as you go, this week, while you can still remember why you dropped the app. In six weeks you won't, and the examiner marks the reasoning, not the data.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: This week.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: This week. Off you go. And no worries about the app, it was a good idea, it's just the wrong term for it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the cost of the things people send back

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about returned goods and what they cost retailers. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Morning, all. Right. Today's topic is the least glamorous thing in retail, and I'd argue the most interesting: what happens to the parcel after somebody decides they don't want it. I'll do the definitions, then the scale of it, then a trial that one of the big groups ran and what it actually showed.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Definitions. Everything you've studied so far moves goods outwards, from the factory to the customer. When a parcel travels the other way, that whole system has its own name, and the term you want is reverse logistics. Reverse, because the goods are going backwards up a chain built to push them forwards.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, the scale. If you ask people at a barbecue how many online orders come back, they'll guess one in twenty. In clothing the real figure is about a quarter? Sorry — a quarter was two seasons ago. On last year's numbers it's closer to thirty per cent.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the reason that number matters so much is that a return is not simply a sale that didn't happen. It's a sale that didn't happen plus a whole second set of labour costs. Somebody has to receive it, open it, inspect it, decide on it, repack it and relist it, and all of that is done by a human being.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's also a customer behaviour driving it that we didn't have ten years ago. Shoppers order the same shirt in three sizes, intending from the outset to keep one. That practice has a name in the trade. It's called bracketing, and on some product lines it's now the majority of orders.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So why do people send things back? The survey answer everybody quotes is quality. And quality does appear, and it's a real category. But it's a distant second. The reason given on about two-thirds of clothing returns is fit. Just fit — it didn't fit.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A quick digression, because it's a good story. There's a warehouse out past Halstow that exists purely to open parcels. Forty people, one job, no shop attached, and it runs on a public holiday roster because the peak is the first week of January. Anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Back to the money. Here's the thing that decides everything downstream. Processing one returned garment costs somewhere between eight and fourteen dollars, and on a lot of fast fashion that is more than the margin on the item was in the first place.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which is why so much of it never goes back on a shelf. And no, it isn't the freight that decides that — freight is cheap and it's getting cheaper. It's the inspection labour. If checking the garment costs more than the garment earns, the rational move for the firm is landfill.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, the trial. The Kellwood group, who specialise in mid-price clothing, spent eighteen months testing what happens if you charge for returns. Flat fee, small, on the app and on the mobile site. Here are four findings, and they're on your sheet as sentences.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first one is the one everybody expects and nobody thinks through. Yes, the return rate dropped, by about a fifth. But total customer spending fell as well, and it fell by enough to wipe out the saving. People didn't return less. They ordered less.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second finding. Of the garments that do come back, roughly half can't be sold as new, and those don't get destroyed any more — they go to clearance outlets, which are a genuinely profitable business now rather than a dumping ground.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third, and this is the one I'd put in an exam answer. The single biggest reduction in returns came from something almost free. They published accurate measurements on every product page. Not size labels, which are meaningless across brands. Actual centimetres, garment by garment.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, the structural one. Returns are still buried inside general operating costs at most firms, so nobody owns the number. Kellwood's finance team realised that nothing changed until returns appeared as a separate line in the accounts. Once it had a line, it had an owner.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, three things to take away from all that. The customer behaviour is rational, the firm's response is rational, and the outcome is a warehouse full of shirts that nobody will ever wear. Next week, packaging, which is the same problem with better public relations.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.explanation: 'Is called' promises a term you may never have met, so predict a single noun and wait for the naming verb. 'That practice has a name in the trade' announces it a clause early. The word is bracketing, and the -ing is part of it.

questions.prompt: - The reason given on about two-thirds of clothing returns is ______.
questions.explanation: 'The reason given' wants a single noun, and the printed fraction tells you to wait for a large figure. Quality is named first and is a genuine category, which is exactly why it is dangerous. She calls it a distant second and then names fit.

questions.prompt:
Money
- Processing one garment can cost more than the item's ______.
questions.explanation: A possessive before the gap forces a singular noun. 'Here's the thing that decides everything downstream' is her loudest emphasis marker in the talk. She prices the handling, then says it exceeds the margin. One word.

questions.prompt: - Where checking costs more than the garment earns, the firm's rational choice is ______.
questions.explanation: The frame wants a destination, and 'rational choice is' means a single noun. She rules freight out with a flat 'no, it isn't', names inspection labour as the real driver, and only then gives the destination. Uncountable, so no -s.

questions.prompt: Charging a return fee cut the return rate, but total customer ______ fell by as much.
questions.explanation: 'Total customer' before the gap forces an uncountable noun about money. She flags the finding as the one everybody expects, then flips it with 'But'. The mark is on the second clause, and the last line explains it: they ordered less.

questions.prompt: Garments that cannot be sold as new are now sent to ______ rather than destroyed.
questions.explanation: 'Sent to' plus 'rather than destroyed' wants a place, and places in this trade are plural. 'Second finding' tells you the sentence has started. She says clearance outlets, so take the two-word chunk and stop before 'which'.

questions.prompt: The largest fall in returns followed the publishing of accurate ______ for each garment.
questions.explanation: 'Accurate' before the gap wants a plural noun for data. She marks this one as exam-worthy, names it, and then rules out size labels in the following clause. Write the plural: the -s is fixed by 'accurate' and by the sense.

questions.prompt: Nothing changed at Kellwood until returns were shown as a separate line in the ______.
questions.explanation: 'A separate line in the' points at a document, and this one is plural in English. 'And fourth, the structural one' announces the last finding. She says the accounts, then explains it: once it had a line, it had an owner.

parts.title: Reporting a bag left on a coach

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man who has left a bag on a coach and the lost property clerk at an Australian coach company. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Barrowfield Coaches, lost property. Deb speaking.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Hi there. I think I've left a backpack on one of your coaches. Yesterday, on the way home. There's a charger in it that I need for work, so I'm keen to get it back.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, let's see what we can do. I'll take the details and put a report on the system for you. We get a lot of these on the regional runs, so don't panic yet. Surname first?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Doust.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Could you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: D. O. U. S. T. Doust. Like the dust in the air, only with an O in the middle.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: D. O. U. S. T. Lovely. Have you got the ticket in front of you?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I have, yeah, it's in my wallet.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There'll be two numbers on it. There's a long one along the top, which is the ticket number, and there's a shorter one underneath the barcode. It's the one under the barcode I want.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Four nine, double two, one six.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Four nine, double two, one six. Got it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And you travelled on the Tuesday, you said?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Tuesday the fifth, yeah.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hang on. The fifth was a Monday. If it was definitely the Tuesday, then you're talking about the twelfth.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The twelfth. You're right, I'm hopeless with dates. That's the trouble with travelling for work, every day looks the same.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And which service were you on?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I got on at Coombe Vale and I got off at Marrindale.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, but the service itself doesn't finish at Marrindale. That coach carries on to Danesford, and the driver books anything left on it in at the far end. So on the report this goes down as the Danesford service.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The Danesford one. Fair enough, I'd never have thought of that. I just assumed the service was named after wherever I got off.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Nobody does. And do you remember the seat?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I was in seat fourteen, the aisle one. The bag was in the rack above it, not down by my feet.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Seat fourteen. That helps, because the cleaners do the racks last. People leave things up there constantly, since you can't see them when you stand up. And what's in it, apart from the charger you mentioned?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: A jacket. No, sorry, not a jacket, a jumper. A green one, my daughter knitted it, which is why I'm ringing at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A green jumper and a charger. That's plenty to identify it by.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, I've got all of that on the system now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, what happens from here, because everybody asks me the same four things. It saves you ringing me back tomorrow.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go on. I'd rather know than keep ringing you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First, how long we hold things. Anything handed in gets logged and kept for twenty-eight days. After that it goes to the charity shop on the corner, and once it's gone there's nothing I can do about it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Twenty-eight days. That's fair enough. I'll set myself a reminder.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It is, but don't sit on it. Second thing, where you pick it up. It used to be the ticket office at the terminal, which suited everybody. Since March it's been the depot out on Fenwick Road, past the roundabout.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The depot. Is that open on a Saturday?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Saturday mornings only, eight until twelve, and there's one bloke on, so ring the bell and wait. Allow yourself an hour, honestly, because they're digging the road up out there.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third thing, and this one catches people out. Bring your licence. Not the ticket. The ticket's no use to me, anybody can print a ticket. I need a photo and a name that matches the report.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Licence, not ticket. I'd have taken the ticket.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: They all do. And last, we let you know either way. If the driver's booked it in, you'll get a text tonight. If nothing's come in by Friday, you'll get a text telling you that as well, so please don't ring us every morning.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's good of you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's easier for us, honestly. Right, that's the report lodged. Your reference is the same number off the ticket, so quote that if you do ring, and it saves us both five minutes.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Thanks, Deb. Fingers crossed.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: No worries at all. Somebody will be in touch tonight either way.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt:
BARROWFIELD COACHES — LOST PROPERTY REPORT

Example
Item: a backpack

Surname: **1** ______
Booking reference: **2** ______
Date of travel: Tuesday **3** ______ October
Service to: **4** ______
Seat: **5** ______
Also inside: a green **6** ______ and a charger
questions.explanation: Predict a surname and get ready to write letters, not words. Her request to spell it is the cue. He gives five letters cleanly and then hands you a check on it by comparing the name to an ordinary word.

questions.prompt:
BARROWFIELD COACHES — LOST PROPERTY REPORT

Example

Surname: **1** ______
Booking reference: **2** ______
Date of travel: Tuesday **3** ______ October
Service to: **4** ______
Seat: **5** ______
Also inside: a green **6** ______ and a charger
questions.explanation: Predict digits. She spends a whole turn telling you there are two numbers on the ticket and which one she wants, so the constraint arrives before the value. The one under the barcode is the short one, and double two means two of them.

questions.prompt:
BARROWFIELD COACHES — LOST PROPERTY REPORT

Example

Surname: **1** ______
Booking reference: **2** ______
Date of travel: Tuesday **3** ______ October
Service to: **4** ______
Seat: **5** ______
Also inside: a green **6** ______ and a charger
questions.explanation: October and Tuesday are printed, so predict a bare date. He gives one and she overrules him with a reason: that date was a Monday. Hang on is the cue, and the value that survives is hers, not his.

questions.prompt:
BARROWFIELD COACHES — LOST PROPERTY REPORT

Example
