Surname: **1** ______
Booking reference: **2** ______
Date of travel: Tuesday **3** ______ October
Service to: **4** ______
Seat: **5** ______
Also inside: a green **6** ______ and a charger
questions.explanation: The printed words are service to, which means the coach's destination and not his. He names two towns of his own and neither is the answer. She then says outright what the report calls this service.

questions.prompt:
BARROWFIELD COACHES — LOST PROPERTY REPORT

Example
Item: a backpack

Surname: **1** ______
Booking reference: **2** ______
Date of travel: Tuesday **3** ______ October
Service to: **4** ______
Seat: **5** ______
Also inside: a green **6** ______ and a charger
questions.explanation: Predict a small number. Her question about the seat is the cue and the value is the first thing he says. The rack and the floor come afterwards and neither is a number, so nothing here competes with it.

questions.prompt:
BARROWFIELD COACHES — LOST PROPERTY REPORT

Example
Item: a backpack

Surname: **1** ______
Booking reference: **2** ______
Date of travel: Tuesday **3** ______ October
Service to: **4** ______
Seat: **5** ______
Also inside: a green **6** ______ and a charger
questions.explanation: Green and a charger are printed, so predict one clothing noun. He names the wrong garment and takes it back inside the same breath. No, sorry is the cue, and the word after it is the one that goes in the box.

questions.prompt: How long is lost property kept before it is given away?
questions.explanation: The stem asks how long, so predict a number and a unit. First is her own numbering and it opens the answer. The period is stated once, in words, and what happens afterwards is the proof you heard the right figure.

questions.prompt: Where must the backpack be collected from?
questions.explanation: Predict a place. Second thing announces it. She names the old collection point first, in the past tense, and then gives the current one with a date attached. Since March is what tells you which is live.

questions.prompt: What must Nick show when he collects the bag?
questions.explanation: Predict a document. Third thing announces it and bring your licence is the instruction. The ticket is named immediately afterwards under a not, and his own next turn shows you exactly which mistake the item is built on.

questions.prompt: How will the company let Nick know either way?
questions.explanation: Predict a method of contact. And last is the marker. The method is named twice, once for good news and once for bad, which is why the answer is safe even if you miss the first half of the sentence.

parts.title: Volunteer briefing at the Northgate Community Kitchen

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a volunteer coordinator briefing a group of new volunteers on their first evening at a community kitchen. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to sixteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to sixteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hi, everyone. I'm Dana, I run the volunteer side of things here, and this is the twenty minutes where I tell you everything and you remember about a third of it. That's fine. It's all on a sheet by the door as well.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, numbers first, because they surprise people. When I started here we were putting out six hundred meals a week and that felt like a lot. As of this fall we're at nine hundred, out of the same kitchen, with the same four stoves.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You'll report to whoever's on as shift lead. Some evenings that's Priya, tomorrow it's a guy called Halloran, and I'll spell that, because everybody gets it wrong. H. A. L. O. — no, sorry, there are two L's in there. Let me do that again. H. A. double L. O. R. A. N.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Shifts. There are two of them. The morning one is seven till noon and it's mostly baking and prep. The afternoon shift, which is the one most of you signed up for, starts at 3.30 and runs until we're done, which is usually somewhere around eight.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: What to wear. We used to ask everybody to bring an apron, and you really don't need to any more — there's a whole rack of them by the door. What you do need, and I will send you home over this, is closed-toe shoes. It's a kitchen. There are hot pans in it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Donations. Everybody assumes we're short of food. We're honestly not. This city is extremely generous and there's a truck outside most mornings. What we are permanently short of is freezer space. If you know anybody with a spare chest freezer, I would like their number.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Age. We love having students, we really do, and we ask for one thing: anybody under sixteen has to be signed in by an adult who then stays in the building. Not out in the parking lot. In the building.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the housekeeping done. Anything you forget is on the sheet taped inside the pantry door, and nobody here has ever been in trouble for asking the same question twice.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the briefing, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. Deliveries, because about half of you signed up to drive. We run four routes a week — Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Thursday's been going since the week this kitchen opened, so it is not the new one, whatever the sign-up sheet told you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And everybody assumes Thursday's the long one, because it goes right out to the county line. It isn't. Friday's longer by a good hour. What Thursday is, is the run I'm forever begging people to drive. If you can only do one route a month, make it that one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The walk-in cooler now. There's a parka hanging on the hook beside the door. Wear it, don't wear it, that's entirely up to you. I'd say most people last about four minutes in there without it, and then they come out and put it on.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Two things that are not up to you. Do not prop that door open, however much you're carrying, because it wrecks the compressor and it costs us a fortune. And nobody goes into the walk-in on their own. Not ever. If I'm not around, grab whoever is.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Drivers, before you go anywhere, come to the office and pick up your route sheet. One piece of paper, addresses in order, door codes on the back. Please don't work off your cell phone. The addresses change on a Tuesday and your phone doesn't know that.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The van, while we're on the subject, is a stick shift, it is older than several of you, and the trick with the back door is that you lift it before you pull it. Everybody in this room will learn that the hard way exactly once.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: One last thing, because somebody always asks. We cook lunch and we cook dinner. We have never once done breakfast, and between you and me we never will, because there is nobody on this earth who wants to be dicing onions at five in the morning.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Aprons are on the rack, the tablet by the door is how you clock in and out, and I'll be somewhere near the stoves if it all goes sideways. Thank you for coming. We genuinely cannot do this without you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt:
NORTHGATE COMMUNITY KITCHEN — VOLUNTEER BRIEFING
What we do
- Meals cooked each week at the moment: ______
questions.explanation: 'At the moment' in the frame warns you the figure will be updated, so predict two numbers and expect the second. 'As of this fall' is the switch. She gives the old figure first and marks it as old with 'when I started here'. Write the current one.

questions.prompt: - Report to the shift lead. Surname: ______
questions.explanation: 'Surname' tells you before the audio that this is transcription, not comprehension. 'I'll spell that' is the cue to put your pen down and take letters. She spells it wrong, says so, and restarts with 'double L'. Take the second run, not a patched first one.

questions.prompt:
Shifts
- The afternoon shift starts at ______.
questions.explanation: 'Starts at' plus 'afternoon' predicts an afternoon clock time, which rules out the first time she gives. She describes the morning shift first and labels it as the morning one. The printed word 'afternoon' is doing all the work here.

questions.prompt:
What to wear
- Everyone on a shift must wear ______.
questions.explanation: 'Must wear' predicts a piece of clothing, and she offers two. The first is explicitly withdrawn: you don't need to bring one any more. 'What you do need' is the endorsement, and the item after it is the answer. The hyphenated compound counts as one word.

questions.prompt:
Donations
- The kitchen is always short of ______.
questions.explanation: The printed frame's own words, 'short of', are spoken twice and attached to the wrong thing the first time. Predict a noun phrase, and wait: 'What we are permanently short of' is the endorsement. Two words, and neither of them takes an -s.

questions.prompt:
Age
- Volunteers under ______ must be signed in by an adult.
questions.explanation: 'Under' plus a printed rule predicts an age in the teens, so a figure over about eighteen would be a mishearing you could reject as you wrote it. 'We ask for one thing' announces the rule, and the whole condition arrives in one clause. Write the figure alone.

questions.prompt: What does Dana say about the Thursday delivery run?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect all three to be spoken. She kills C before the question even starts and A with a flat 'it isn't'. 'What Thursday is, is' is the endorsement frame, and what follows it is a plea for drivers, not a fact about distance.

questions.prompt: What does Dana tell volunteers about the walk-in cooler?
questions.explanation: The stem asks what she tells them, so predict an instruction and expect optional things nearby. 'Two things that are not up to you' is the frame. One instruction is a prohibition on the door; the other is the rule about going in alone, and only one of them is an option here.

questions.prompt: What do drivers collect from the office before every run?
questions.explanation: The stem predicts a thing, small enough to carry, and the limit is two words. 'Before you go anywhere' announces it. She says 'pick up' where your page says 'collect', so the printed verb is never spoken and you must listen for the meaning.

questions.prompt: Which meal has the kitchen never provided?
questions.explanation: 'Which meal' fixes the slot to one word from a very small set, so predict the three and wait. 'One last thing' announces the closing item. She names the two they do cook first, then the negative. The answer is the one attached to 'never'.

parts.title: Reviewing field work: a sand-dune vegetation survey

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Nell and Bethan, going over a weekend of dune field work with their tutor, Doctor Kessel. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right, sit down, both of you. So the dune survey. I've been through the sheets you handed in, and I want to start with something that isn't your fault. There's a lot in here that works, and two things that really don't.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The tide.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The tide. You laid your first transect out at low water on the Saturday, and by the time you'd finished quadrat six the sea was over your first three.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We did get the readings, though. All six of them, before the water came up.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Six is short for a transect anyway. The handbook says ten.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Six would have been survivable. The problem is different. A dune transect is meant to be a gradient from wet to dry, and yours goes wet to dry and then back to wet. It doesn't describe anything.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we redo it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You redo it, and this time you start at the top of the dune and walk down, so the sea can't catch you. And take the tape out before you take the quadrat frame out, not after.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Can I ask about the grid references? We lost the ones for transect two.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You didn't lose them. You never took them.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We took them on my phone. I had signal in the car park, and then nothing at all on the beach.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: On a phone with no signal, on a beach. Look, it doesn't matter how now. What matters is that transect two has no location, so it isn't a transect, it's a list of plants.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the counts? Bethan and I got different numbers in the same quadrat.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Twice. Marram grass, quadrat four. I had thirty and Nell had eleven.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Were you counting shoots, or were you counting plants? Because those are two completely different numbers, and they both went in the same column.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Shoots.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Plants. Or clumps, I suppose.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: There it is. Marram spreads underground, so one plant can put up forty shoots. Neither of you is wrong. You just never wrote down which of the two you were counting, and that goes in your method before you go back.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: What about transect three? We never got to it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Leave it. Three transects was ambitious for a weekend, and two good ones beat three rushed ones. Write in your limitations that you planned three and ran two, and say why.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Ross's group did three. We could borrow theirs.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You could, and then it'd be Ross's field work with your name on the front of it. No. Two is honest. An examiner can spot a borrowed transect from the handwriting on the sheet.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And is any of it any good?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Your species identification is the best I've had from a second year. Bethan, you keyed out two sedges that I'd have had to look up. That's the part I'd build the write-up around, not the transects.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. The resurvey. Let's get the practical side fixed now, so that you don't repeat any of this in a fortnight. I've got twenty minutes, so I'll ask and you answer.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We're free the weekend after next.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You're not going at a weekend. The wardens only open the gate to vehicles on a Wednesday, and you're carrying quadrats and a tape.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Wednesday it is, then.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Wednesday. And be on site by nine, because the light goes early in November and half your photographs from last time are unusable.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The photographs. What do you actually want in them?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Every quadrat, from directly above, with a scale bar lying along the edge of the frame. Without a scale bar the photograph is a nice picture of some grass.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Scale bar. We've got one.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Do we record everything to species? The handbook says species.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The handbook is written for a whole-summer project. For yours, genus is fine for the grasses, and it'll save you an hour a transect. Species only for the sedges, because that's where your marks are.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: How many of us do we need?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Four. Two on the tape and two recording.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Three would do it if you're organised, but four is safer with the tide. Take four.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: I'll type the data up when we get home.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Don't. Type it into the shared sheet in the car park before you leave the site, while you can still read your own handwriting and remember what your abbreviations meant.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Car park. Fine.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And send me the two transects by the Friday. Not the write-up. Just the numbers. I'd rather see two honest transects on the Friday than a polished excuse on the Monday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt: Why does Doctor Kessel say the first transect cannot be used?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the flooding to be described before the fault is named. He says outright that six quadrats would have been survivable, then gives the real problem: a gradient that runs wet, dry and wet again. That shape is what different states of the tide produces.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with the second transect?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and notice the correction two turns earlier: they did not lose the references, they never took them. He then refuses to discuss how and says what matters, which is the signpost. No location means no transect, and the species list is exactly what survives.

questions.prompt: Why did the two students record different numbers?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and treat the tutor's question as the item. He asks shoots or plants, gets two different answers, and says there it is. Neither of you is wrong rules out any careless-counting option in four words, and the fix he gives is a recording instruction, not a counting one.

questions.prompt: What does Doctor Kessel advise about the third transect?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect an offer to be made and refused, because that is the rhythm of the whole tutorial. Leave it is the verdict, and the instruction that follows tells them to write the gap up as a limitation. Borrowing from Ross is proposed afterwards and killed in one turn.

questions.prompt: What does Doctor Kessel say was the strongest part of their work?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect one thing to be praised and one to be excluded in the same sentence. Best I've had from a second year is the endorsement, the two sedges are the evidence, and not the transects at the end removes the option a learner is most likely to still be holding.

questions.prompt: The resurvey must take place on a ______ because of the vehicle gate.
questions.explanation: Predict a day, because a is printed and the printed reason is a gate. Nell offers a weekend and he refuses it in five words. Bethan's confirmation is your last warning that the answer is arriving, and he repeats the day on its own to open the next turn.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about the failure of reinforced concrete structures. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, settle down. Today, reinforced concrete, and specifically why so much of it built in the last century is now coming apart. I'll set up the chemistry, then take you through the two attack mechanisms, then a survey of road bridges, and I'll finish with an argument you may not agree with.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Start with why we reinforce at all. Concrete is superb in compression. Squash it and it just gets on with it. But pull it apart and it's hopeless, because concrete is weak in tension, so we cast steel bars into the parts of a beam that are being stretched.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, steel in the open air rusts. Steel inside concrete does not, and the reason is chemical rather than physical. Fresh concrete is strongly alkaline, and that alkalinity grows a microscopically thin oxide film on the surface of every bar. We call that film the passive layer, and while it holds, nothing happens at all.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So the whole subject reduces to one question: what destroys the passive layer? And there are two answers, and only two that matter.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first is slow and it is universal. Carbon dioxide from the air works its way in through the pores and reacts with the alkali, and the concrete gradually stops being alkaline from the outside inwards. That process is carbonation, and you can watch its front advance with a spray bottle of indicator.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The second is faster and it is local. People assume this one is coastal — the sea, the spray, the marine structures. It is far more often the road. What breaks the film here is chlorides, and inland they arrive by the lorryload every winter as de-icing salt.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which brings me to the single most important number on any drawing, and the one that gets cut first when a job is running late. It isn't the strength of the mix. It's how far the bar sits back from the surface, and the word for that is cover.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A quick aside, because it makes the point better than I can. There's a footbridge at Merridge where the drawings specified forty millimetres and the site poured it at twelve, and you can read the whole story off the underside without any instruments at all. Anyway, back to the mechanism.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Once the film is gone, the bar corrodes, and rust takes up several times the volume of the steel it came from. So the bar swells, the concrete around it cracks along the line of the bar, and eventually a slab of the surface detaches. The word you want for that detaching is spalling.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right — the survey. Eleven hundred road bridges, inspected on a common protocol over four years, which is the largest consistent data set anybody in this country has.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the finding that surprised people was where the damage starts. Everybody expected the deck surface, because that's where the salt lands. Sorry — expected is wrong, everybody assumed it, which is different. In practice the damage starts at the expansion joints, because that is where the salty water gets underneath.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: On repair, the survey is blunter still. The only intervention that stopped corrosion outright, rather than slowing it, was cathodic protection, which works by making the whole reinforcement cage electrically negative so the steel simply cannot give up ions.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Patching, by contrast, has a failure mode that nobody expects. You cut out the damaged concrete, you put new alkaline material back, and the repaired area is now healthier than everything around it. Which drives the corrosion straight to the boundary. New damage appears within about two years, and not where you would look for it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh — hang on. I said the damage appears at the patch. Let me be precise, because it matters for your coursework: it appears just outside it, at the patch edges. The patch itself is fine. It's the ring around the patch that goes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the argument, and then I'll let you go. Everyone in this field talks about better materials, and the materials are not the problem. Self-healing mixes, stainless reinforcement, coatings — all real, all expensive, none of them fitted to the structures we already own. What actually decides the life of a bridge is maintenance.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which is a budgeting argument dressed up as an engineering one, and that is exactly why nobody wins it. Next week, timber, which fails honestly and in public.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman hiring equipment to sand a floor and an assistant at a tool hire shop. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Kilnmore Tool Hire, Wes speaking.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Oh, hello. I'm after hiring a floor sander. We've taken the carpet up in the front room and the boards underneath are in a bit of a state. Somebody varnished them in about nineteen seventy and nobody has touched them since.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: No worries, we do a lot of those this time of year. I'll start a booking and we'll sort you out. Can I grab a surname?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Quennell.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: How's that spelt?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Q. U. E. double N. E. double L. Quennell. Nobody gets it first time, don't worry.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Q. U. E. double N. E. double L. There you go, first time. And a contact number?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It's oh seven, double one, four, three six two, nine oh four.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Oh seven, double one, four, three six two, nine oh four. Got that.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Right, machines. For a room that size there are two you could take. There's the belt sander, which is the smaller one, and there's the drum sander.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Which do people usually go for? I've never done anything like this before, so I'm in your hands.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: For boards that have never been done, the drum, every time. The belt one's fine for touching up a bit of skirting, but honestly you'd be there all weekend with it. I'd put you down for the drum.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The drum one, then. I'll take your word for it, because I certainly don't want to be doing it twice.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And when do you want it? We're open seven till five, and Saturdays till one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Saturday morning, if you've got one free. Actually, no, hang on. My husband's got the car on the Saturday, so that's no good at all. Friday afternoon would be much better.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Friday afternoon it is. That gets you the whole weekend on a two-day rate, which is a bit of luck for you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And what do you need off me when I come in?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: There's a deposit. It was eighty pounds right up until the spring, but we've dropped it to sixty now the machines are newer. You get it straight back when the machine comes back in one piece.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sixty. That's fine, I'll bring the card. Do you take it back off the card straight away, or is it held?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And I'd take the edger while you're at it. The drum won't get within four inches of the skirting, so without one you'll have a border of old varnish all the way round the room and you'll be on your knees with a scraper.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then I'd better have an edger as well, hadn't I.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Good decision. So that's the drum, the edger, Friday afternoon, and I'll put the sheets aside for you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Now, the costs, because they're not all charged the same way and people do get caught out.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Go ahead, I'm writing this down.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The drum sander's thirty-five pounds a day. There's a weekend rate of fifty for the two days, which is what you'll actually be on, but the figure that goes on the booking form is thirty-five.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thirty-five on the form. Right.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The edger's eighteen a day, and that one doesn't live in the shop. It's in the yard round the back, so come to the yard gate rather than the counter, or you'll only get sent round anyway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The yard gate, not the counter. Noted.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Sheets are two pounds each. Take a dozen, take twenty, it makes no odds, because you only pay for the ones you use. Bring the rest back unopened and we don't charge you for them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's decent of you. Everywhere else I rang wanted paying for the lot up front.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's not generosity, it's that nobody on earth can guess how many they'll need. Last thing, the extractor. It comes free with the sander and you'd be mad not to take it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: It's fine on floorboards and old paint. Do not use it on plaster, though. Plaster dust kills the motor stone dead, and that's a two hundred pound repair, and that one does come out of your deposit.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Floorboards yes, plaster no. Understood. I'll keep it well away from the walls.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: You've got it. I'll have the paperwork ready for Friday, so you can be in and out in ten minutes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Thanks very much, that's all really clear. I was dreading this phone call, to be honest with you.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: No worries at all. See you Friday afternoon.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A guide's introduction at the Norland Museum of Making

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a guide introducing a group of visitors to the ground floor of a small museum. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hello, and welcome to Norland. I'm Priya, I'll be with you for the first half hour or so. There's a floor plan in the middle of your leaflet, and I would get that out now, because this building was three separate workshops before anyone thought of turning it into a museum, and it does not make a great deal of sense from the inside.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. We're all standing in the doorway with the street behind us, and reception is the desk straight in front of you. Keep that desk ahead of you. Every left and right I give in the next few minutes assumes you are facing it from where you are now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The first door on your left, just before you draw level with the desk, is the cloakroom. Bags bigger than a shopping bag have to go in there, I'm afraid, and it's free, and there's a code on the back of your ticket.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Directly opposite the cloakroom, so on your right, is the gift shop. It's open the whole time we are, and it is very much smaller than everybody expects, so if there are twelve of you in it, it is full.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now walk past reception and out into the courtyard, which is the open square in the middle of your plan. On the far side of it, straight ahead as you come out, is the print room. That was the boiler house until the refit, and one of the older guidebooks still calls it that, so do ignore your guidebook.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: From the print room, turn right and follow the covered walk. The room in the far corner is the toy gallery. No — sorry, the toy gallery is upstairs, I always do that. The room in that corner is the clock gallery, and it ticks, loudly, and some people find it unbearable.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Then keep going down the right-hand side. You'll pass the stairs and then the lift, and neither of those is a question, they're printed on your plan already. Right at the bottom of that side, in the corner nearest the door you came in by, is the lecture theatre.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the ground floor. Upstairs is one long room running the whole length of the building, and you genuinely cannot get lost in it, which is the entire reason I have spent all this time down here with a plan instead of just walking you round it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the introduction, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, what's actually on this week. Four things, and two of them cost money. I'll be honest with you, the two that cost money are the two I would do, and the two that are free are the two everybody turns up for, which is how it always goes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The handling table runs on Saturdays. That's the one where children get to pick things up, and it starts at 10.30 and it runs until we run out of children, usually about one. Five and over, and please stay with them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The print workshop. Now, people expect that to be the Saturday one as well, because everything else on this list is, and it isn't. The print workshop is Sundays, two o'clock, and it takes an hour and a half, and you do come out of it covered in ink.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: It was four pounds last year and that barely covered the ink, so from this month it's six pounds, which includes the paper and whatever you print going home with you in a tube.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The building tour is Thursday mornings, eleven o'clock, and that one is completely free. We meet by the sundial in the courtyard, not at reception, because reception is where everybody instinctively waits and then nobody can hear a word I am saying over the till.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And late opening. Now, the poster in the window still says the last Friday of the month, and that poster is wrong and I have told them. It's the last Thursday of the month, until nine, with music in the courtyard.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, that's me. Take a plan on your way through, mind the step going out into the courtyard because everybody catches it, and if a clock stops while you are standing in the corner gallery, I promise you it isn't anything you did.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.explanation: Predict a room on the left of the corridor, before the printed desk. 'The first door on your left' announces it and the room is named at the end of the same clause. No rival is offered, so this is the item that confirms your orientation was right.

Predict the room on the far side of the printed courtyard. 'Straight ahead as you come out' places it. She names it, then gives the name it had before the refit and marks that name as old. A guidebook she tells you to ignore is not an answer.

Only the bottom of the right-hand side is left. She names the stairs and the lift first and tells you they are already printed, which is the clearest possible instruction not to write them. The answer comes after 'right at the bottom of that side'.

parts.title: Preparing a symposium talk on sleep and study

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Marisa and Frankie, preparing a symposium talk with their supervisor, Doctor Vance. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: OK. The symposium is in nine days, so let's make this useful rather than encouraging. Talk me through what you've actually got.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twenty-two slides. Literature first, then the method, then our results, and then a section on what it means for the university.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Twenty-two slides. Right. And which of those four sections does your audience already know?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The literature. They're all sleep people. Half of them wrote it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We were told to review the literature, though. It's in the assignment description.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You were told to review it in the paper. In the talk, everybody in that room can recite it, and you'll spend six of your minutes telling forty specialists what they published themselves. One slide, then get to your own data.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the method? That's four slides at the moment.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The method's fine. Long, but fine, and nobody in that room will question it. Leave it alone for now and come back to it if you run short.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So how do we open? I had a question, like, how many of you got seven hours last night?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Open with the finding. Just say it. The students who moved their alarm an hour later gained forty minutes of sleep and lost nothing on the tests.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Ooh, or we open with the video of the sleep lab. Everybody loves the sleep lab.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Everybody does love the sleep lab, and it will eat ninety seconds and tell them nothing a still picture couldn't. Open with the number. Frankie's sentence, exactly the way she just said it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the graph? The one with the two lines on it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The two lines is the right graph and the wrong version of it. You've got a legend, gridlines, a title, axis labels in eight point, and somewhere underneath all that, two lines. Delete everything except the two lines and make them thick enough to read from the back of the room.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. And timing?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: We've got twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Fifteen. It's fifteen this year, they cut it when they added the poster session.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: It's fifteen on the program, and fifteen means twelve, because the chair takes three for questions and she will not let you run over. Build a twelve-minute talk and rehearse it with a clock.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Twelve. Right.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And send me the slides by Monday night. Not Tuesday. The technician loads everything on Tuesday morning, and if yours isn't in the folder you're presenting off your own laptop, which never works in that room.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. You've got five things left that you want in there and about four minutes of room. Let's put each one somewhere, and then you can stop arguing about it on the bus.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The method diagram. The flow one, with the four weeks across the top.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That one goes up. It's the only thing in your whole talk that can't be said in a sentence, and that is exactly what a screen is for.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Sample sizes next. We've got a table with the numbers for each of the three groups.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Doctor Vance said last week that every talk needs its numbers on screen.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: I said every paper needs its numbers. Nobody has ever read a table of three columns from twenty feet away, so put that one in the handout and leave the screen alone.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The quotes. We've got two really good ones from the diary entries.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Read them. Don't show them. If a quotation is up there the room reads it faster than you can say it and then stops listening to you. Two quotations, read aloud, are thirty of the best seconds in your talk.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Limitations. We've got a whole slide on them.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You've got a whole slide apologizing. Take it down, and put the two real ones into a sentence when you get to the findings. On a slide a limitation looks like a confession. In a sentence it looks like judgment.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the references?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Nobody wants a wall of references at the end of a twelve-minute talk. Put them on the handout in six point, and if somebody wants one they will ask you afterwards, which is a much better conversation anyway.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: So that's one slide gone, one added, and the graph rebuilt from scratch.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And nine days. Send them Monday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how a new word gets into a dictionary

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about how new words are added to dictionaries. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: All right. Everybody asks the same question about this job, which is: who decides? So today I want to take that apart. First the evidence editors actually work from, then the tests a candidate word has to pass, and then, at the end, an argument about what a dictionary is for. That last part is where we'll disagree.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The evidence first. Nobody sits in a room deciding what English ought to contain. Editors work from an enormous searchable body of real language, gathered from print, broadcast, transcribed talk, and now the web. The technical name for that body of material is a corpus, and the good ones run to billions of words.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Inside that corpus, the unit that matters is the individual recorded use. One sentence, dated, with its source attached. Those are citations, and the whole trade runs on them. An editor doesn't argue about a word. An editor counts them.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: How many do you need? The old working rule was ten independent citations. Sorry, ten is what I was taught, and it's out of date. Most houses now want twenty before they'll even open a file, and they want them from unrelated writers.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, where do candidate words come from? Several routes, and one of them fills more slots than the rest. You take two existing words and fuse them, keeping the front of one and the back of the other. We used to call those portmanteau words, after a Victorian joke, and some of my colleagues still do. The current term is a blend.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A digression, because somebody always raises it. There is no committee. There's no vote, no ceremony, no letter of admission. It's a spreadsheet and an editor with a deadline, and if that disappoints you, I'd say it should reassure you instead. Nobody has ever received a letter about it. Anyway, back to the tests.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Three tests, and a word has to pass all three. Frequency, which is just how often. Spread, which is how many different kinds of writer use it. And the third one, which is the one that kills most candidates, is durability. Is it still there in five years?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And a point people find genuinely surprising: nothing is ever taken out. A big historical dictionary doesn't delete. It isn't a question of space, and it isn't squeamishness. The word simply gets tagged obsolete and stays on the page, because somebody reading an old book still needs it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: OK. Four observations about the practice, and these are the sentences on your sheet. I'll number them as I go, so if you lose your place, count along with me instead of reading ahead. Each one surprises students, and each one has a practical consequence for anybody who works with text for a living.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First. The words that give editors the most trouble are the ones born in conversation, because talk leaves no dated record. A word can be in every playground in the country for a decade before anybody writes it down, and the first citation is then wrong by ten years.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second. The volunteer reading programs that built the great dictionaries still exist, and I'm fond of them, but they're no longer where the material comes from. Most of what lands on an editor's desk this morning was pulled out of digital archives overnight by software.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third, and this is the commonest reason for a rejection. A word gets turned down when everybody using it works in the same place. If the citations all come from one industry, it fails the spread test, however frequent it is inside that world.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, the argument I promised. A dictionary does tell you which spelling is commoner, and people take that as a ruling. It isn't. The entry records use. It doesn't grant permission, and it never has. Nobody at any dictionary has the standing to permit or forbid a word.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So: evidence, three tests, and a book that describes rather than instructs. Next week we'll look at what happens to a word after it's in, which is where the real fights are. Bring the two entries I posted, and read the short piece on labelling as well, because that argument is this one in miniature.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt:
NEW WORDS IN DICTIONARIES
Evidence
- Editors work from a large searchable collection of real language, called a ______.
questions.explanation: 'Called a' promises a term and the article tells you it is singular and countable. 'The technical name for that body of material' announces it. He says corpus. Nothing here is guessable, so the naming phrase is the whole of your warning.

questions.prompt: - Individual dated examples of a word in use are ______.
questions.explanation: 'Are' after a plural subject forces a plural noun, so the -s is decided before he speaks. 'The unit that matters' announces the term a clause ahead. He says citations and then repeats the idea as counting them. Write the plural.

questions.prompt: - Most publishers now want at least ______ independent examples before opening a file.
questions.explanation: The printed 'now' warns you an older figure is coming, and 'at least' fixes this as a bare number. He gives ten, calls it what he was taught, and says it is out of date. The current figure is twenty. Digits only.

questions.prompt:
Routes in
- A word made by fusing the front of one word to the back of another is now called a ______.
questions.explanation: The printed 'now' is the whole item: it tells you an older name exists and is not wanted. He gives the older one first, attributes it to a Victorian joke, and says some colleagues still use it. The current term arrives last.

questions.prompt:
The three tests
- Frequency, spread, and third: ______, meaning the word is still in use five years later.
questions.explanation: Two of the three tests are printed, so predict a third abstract noun in the same shape. 'Three tests' announces a countable list, and he tells you which one kills most candidates. He names it, then paraphrases it as still being there in five years.

questions.prompt: - Words are never removed; they are simply tagged ______.
questions.explanation: 'Tagged' takes a label, so predict a single describing word rather than a noun. He spends two clauses on why they are not deleted, and both of those are negatives. The label itself comes last, and it is the only word that fits after 'tagged'.

questions.prompt: The hardest words to date are the ones that begin in ______, which leaves no written record.
questions.explanation: 'Begin in' plus 'no written record' wants an uncountable noun that is the opposite of writing. The printed phrase is never spoken: he says born in conversation, and then talk. Predict the meaning in the preview and listen for anything carrying it.

questions.prompt: Most material now reaches editors from ______ rather than from volunteer readers.
questions.explanation: The frame rules the readers out, so predict the modern source. He praises the reading programmes first and even says he is fond of them, which is a concession, not the answer. The mark sits after 'but'. Two words, plural.

questions.prompt: A word is usually rejected when all its users belong to one ______.
questions.explanation: 'One' before the gap forces a singular countable noun. He signals this as the commonest reason for rejection, describes it in plain words first, and only then names it. The named test, spread, is not the answer; the group is.

questions.prompt: An entry records how a word is used; it does not grant ______.
questions.explanation: 'Grant' takes an abstract uncountable noun, and the semicolon sets it against recording. He offers the spelling ruling first, agrees people read it that way, and flatly denies it. The keyed noun is spoken in exactly the printed frame.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is the IELTS-style Listening practice test. You will hear four separate recordings and answer questions on each. Each recording is played once only. You will be given time to read the questions before each recording and a short time to check your answers afterwards. The test has four parts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man arranging a furniture delivery and a scheduling clerk at a store in the United States. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.

lines.speaker: narrator

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Hartsmoor Furniture, delivery scheduling. This is Marisol.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Hi. I'm calling to set up delivery on a couch. It came into the warehouse last week, I got the email about it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sure, let's get you on a truck. Can I start with a last name?

lines.speaker: s2

lines.speaker: s1

lines.speaker: s2

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: R. A. S. M. U. double S. E. N. Thank you. And there should be an order number on that email.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Let me pull it up. Okay, here we go. Seven one two, eight four. Hang on, no, that's the quote number from when I came into the store. The order number's the one below it. Double four, one nine, oh three.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Double four, one nine, oh three. That's the one, I've got your couch right here on the screen.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, dates. We're only in your neighborhood on Thursdays, so it's a Thursday whatever we do.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Thursday's fine. The sooner the better, honestly, we've been sitting on the floor for a month.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: I hear that a lot. The fifteenth is our next run out there, but that truck's already full. The one after is the twenty-second of May, and I can get you on it.

lines.speaker: s2

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Great. Now, timing. The crew starts at eight, and I originally had you down for the morning run.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: But they're doing a whole building over on Ash Street that morning, so realistically you're looking at from 1.30 onwards. I'd rather tell you now than have you waiting in all day for nothing.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: From one thirty. That's fine, I'll work from home that afternoon.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Perfect. Now, the building itself. Is there an elevator?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: There is, but it's tiny. The couch is going to have to come up the stairs.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's no problem, they do stairs all day. Which entrance do they want?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Not the front one, whatever you do. The front entrance opens straight onto the main street and there's nowhere to stop a truck. They want the rear entrance, off the parking lot.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Rear entrance, off the lot. I'll put that on the ticket in capitals, because otherwise they will try the front.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if nobody's home? Some buildings have a front desk we can use, but yours doesn't, does it?

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: No desk, no. Leave it with a neighbor if you have to. Apartment 4B, she's retired and she is always, always in.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Apartment 4B. Got it. Okay, you are booked.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Now, a few things about the day itself, because these are the ones that surprise people.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Go ahead, I'm listening.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Packaging. The crew unwraps everything in the room it's going in, and every piece of it goes back out with them. You do not end up with a mountain of cardboard in your apartment.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: That's a relief. The last place we bought from left it all stacked flat in the hallway for a week.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: We used to do exactly that, years ago, and the building managers hated us for it. Now it all goes back on the truck and gets recycled at our warehouse rather than in your building's bins.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Good. So what do you need from me before they show up?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Clear the hallway between your front door and the room it's going in. Genuinely, that's all. People take their doors off the hinges for us and it has never once been necessary with a two-seater.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And don't move your car for us either. The crew parks on the street and walks it in. You would not believe how many people spend a morning hunting for another space.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Okay. And what about the old couch? Can they take that away?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: They can't, I'm afraid, not on a delivery run. What most people do is call the thrift store over on Fenmore. They'll come out for anything that's clean, and they don't charge you for it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: There's been talk of us starting a removal service of our own, mind you. There's been talk of that for about three years now.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Understood. And the balance on the order?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The balance is due before we load. You'll get a link tonight, you pay it online, and once that clears you're locked in for the twenty-second.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The crew can't take payment, by the way. They don't carry a reader on the truck at all.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Could I just come into the store and pay it at the counter?

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You could try, but they'll send you straight back to the link. The counter can't run money against a delivery order, it's a completely different system.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Online it is. Thanks, that was painless.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: You're very welcome. Thursday the twenty-second, from one thirty, rear entrance.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.text: Now walk up the left-hand side of the oval, past the grandstand. Right in the top corner on that side is the wood chop. No, hang on, that's not right, the wood chop is out on the oval itself. The thing in that top corner is the cooking stage.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Straight across the top of the ground, over on the other side, are the sheep yards. You'll smell those before you see them, and that is where the dog trial runs on the Sunday morning, so it's worth knowing where they are.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And then coming back down the river side, between the sheep yards and the gate, is the medical tent. That corner used to be the fire brigade display and it was for years, so if somebody tells you the truck's in there, it isn't, it's parked out on the road now.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's the ground. It looks enormous on paper and it takes about eight minutes to walk the whole way round, so nobody needs to panic about missing anything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right, what's on and when. It's all in the program, which is two dollars from the information tent and worth it for the map alone. Sunday is much the quieter of the two days, and yes, you can bring the dog on either day, before anybody asks me that again.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: The cooking stage. The demonstration is on the Friday, two o'clock, which surprises people because everything else is on the weekend, but the chef flies out on the Saturday morning and there's nothing anybody can do about that. It's free and there's seating for about eighty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Sheepdog trial, Sunday morning, and that one you do pay for. It's five dollars a head, kids under twelve are free, and every cent of it goes to the flying doctor. Not fifteen, by the way. I've heard people saying fifteen and I have no idea where that started.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the night markets, both evenings, down along the river path with the lights in the trees. They run till late, but last entry is 9.30, because the gates are locked at ten and we have had people wander up at five to ten and be genuinely heartbroken.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Dogs. Look, half this town brings a dog. There's a sign at the gate that says no dogs, and that sign belongs to the sportsground, not to us, and I have asked for it to come down. Dogs are fine here. What we do ask is that anywhere near the sheep yards they're on a lead, and a short one.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And if you want one piece of advice off me. Get here at nine and walk the whole ground before anybody else is awake, because at eleven you will not be able to move. And no, you can't book a seat at the sheepdog trial. It doesn't work like that. You turn up and you stand where you can see.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: That's me. Bins are by the grandstand, there's water at the information tent, and if you lose a child, bring them to us and we'll keep them until somebody claims them. Have a lovely weekend.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part two. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.explanation: Predict the first position, left of the gate and before the printed information tent. 'First thing on your left' announces it and the name lands at the end of the clause. She then lists what is inside, which confirms you heard the right thing.

Predict the mirror of 11, on the other side of the gate. She names the ticket caravan first and says it has never been on the plan. 'What is on your plan' is the switch, and the label follows straight after it.

Predict the top corner on the grandstand side. She names the wood chop, stops, and says it is out on the oval itself, which is not a numbered position. 'The thing in that top corner' is the repair, and the right name follows it.

Predict the other top corner, across from 13. 'Straight across the top of the ground' places it, and the plural verb 'are' tells you the answer is plural before you hear the noun. She then attaches Sunday's dog trial to it, which fixes it in memory.

Only the river side is left, between two things already on your plan. She names it first, then gives the corner's old use and marks it as old with 'used to be'. A truck somebody may tell you about is not on your plan at all.

questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect a sign to be quoted and dismissed. She explains that the no-dogs sign belongs to the sportsground and says dogs are fine here. 'What we do ask' is the endorsement frame, and one place gets a condition attached to it.

parts.title: Working out what a reading list is for

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Owen and Jarrah, discussing a reading list with their lecturer, Doctor Weir. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right, come in, both of you. So, the reading list for the coastal tourism unit. Nine items on it, and you have both told me separately that it's too long, which it is.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Heaps too long. I read four of them before uni started and I still couldn't tell you what the argument of the unit actually is.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That's because four of those nine don't contain an argument. They're on the list for something else entirely. Let's go through the five that matter, because knowing what a source is for is most of the skill in a reading list.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Start with Halloran? That's the one everybody in the seminar keeps quoting.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Halloran is the argument. The whole unit is a response to that chapter, and if you only read one thing properly this semester, make it that one. Twice, with a pen in your hand.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: And the tourism board figures? The annual ones, with all the tables at the back.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: There's no argument in there at all. It's a spreadsheet with a foreword. But it's the only place you'll find bed nights by month for the last ten years, and every essay in this unit needs at least one number out of it.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So we don't read that one, we mine it.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Exactly. Now, the harbour article. Or, sorry, articles, because there are two of them with almost the same title. The one you want is Sandmouth harbour and the winter economy, not Sandmouth harbour since the ferry. The ferry one describes what happened. The winter one asks why.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The winter one.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The winter one, and it's the second argument of the unit. It disagrees with Halloran about who actually benefits from a summer season, and your essay lives in the gap between those two readings.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the old planning report? The green one in the library, the one with no cover.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That one used to be the core reading, back when the council was still working from it. It's been superseded twice since then. Read the summary if you like the history, but nothing in it is current, and nobody will give you marks for citing it as evidence.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Last one on my list. The podcast series.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Doctor Weir put it at the top of the list, so I assumed it was the important one.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: I put it first because it's twenty minutes and it's free, not because it's the best thing on there. It's an interview, it's charming, and it's one person's memory of a town. Listen to it on the bus. Don't cite it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Right. The essay. You've got a choice of two questions this semester, and I want to talk you out of one of them before either of you gets attached to it.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: The one about seasonality?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: That one's fine. It's the second question, the one about resident attitudes, that I'd steer you away from, because you'd need survey data nobody has collected and the pair of you would end up quoting the podcast at me.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So both of us do seasonality?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Both of you do seasonality, and you'll write completely different essays anyway, because Jarrah will argue from the figures and Owen will argue from Halloran. That's fine. That is precisely what a seminar is for.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Can we use the same figures, though? The same table out of the annual report?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: You can use the same table. You can't use the same sentence about it. I've had that go wrong twice this year and it is a very boring conversation to have in my office in November.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And how much of the list do we actually have to read?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: For the essay, three of the nine, properly. For the exam in November, all nine, but skimmed. Those are two completely different jobs, and every year somebody does them the wrong way round and runs out of time.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: When do you actually want the essay?

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: The unit outline says week six. Ignore the outline. It was written before the public holiday moved. It's week seven now, and I've put that on the noticeboard outside my office as well.

lines.speaker: s2
lines.text: Week seven. No worries.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: And bring one page of notes on Halloran to the seminar on Thursday. One page, handwritten, and not a summary you've had generated for you overnight.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Handwritten. Understood.

lines.speaker: s3
lines.text: Handwritten. See you Thursday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt: the Halloran chapter
questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and use the first source to learn her vocabulary. She names the job in four words before saying anything else, and the sentence that follows makes the whole unit a reply to it. Read it twice with a pen is advice about how, not a different verdict.

questions.prompt: the tourism board's annual figures
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and take the opening negative as information, not as a verdict. No argument rules out one letter immediately. Then but turns the sentence, and she says every essay in the unit needs a number from it, which is as strong a statement of usefulness as she makes anywhere.

questions.prompt: the article on the harbour and the winter economy
questions.explanation: Predict a letter, and read the printed stem carefully, because two articles share almost the same title and she corrects herself mid-sentence to separate them. The one that asks why is the second argument of the unit, and your essay is placed in the gap between it and Halloran.

questions.prompt: the old council planning report
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and let the tense decide it. Used to be the core reading is past, and superseded twice is the confirmation. She then licenses the summary for the history and forbids it as evidence, which is exactly the difference between background and a source you can use.

questions.prompt: the podcast series
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and notice that Owen reasons from the order of the list rather than from anything she has said. She explains the ordering as length and cost, describes the source as one person's memory, and closes with two imperatives: listen to it, do not cite it.

questions.prompt: Which essay question does Doctor Weir advise against?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and expect the wrong title to be offered first, by a student, as a guess. She clears it in three words and then names the one she is steering them away from, with two reasons: data nobody has, and the temptation to fall back on the podcast.

questions.prompt: What does Doctor Weir say about the two students using the same source?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and hear the pair of sentences as one answer. You can use the same table sets the permission and you can't use the same sentence sets the limit. Her warning about a boring conversation in November tells you which half of that pair she has been burned by.

questions.prompt: How much of the reading list is needed for the essay?
questions.explanation: Predict a letter and pin the stem's word essay, because she answers for two different tasks in one turn. The essay takes three properly; the exam takes nine skimmed. Her closing remark, that people do them the wrong way round, exists precisely to warn you about this item.

questions.prompt: The essay is now due in week ______.
questions.explanation: Predict a small figure, because week is printed in front of the gap. She names the printed document's date first and then tells you to ignore it, with the reason attached. The number that survives comes with now after it, which is the word that marks a current value.

questions.prompt: Bring one page of ______ on Halloran to Thursday's seminar.
questions.explanation: Predict a plural noun, because one page of is printed and of takes a mass or plural word. The instruction is the first thing in her turn and she repeats the constraint twice afterwards. Handwritten and not generated are conditions on it, not the answer to it.

parts.title: Lecture: how the railways gave us the clock

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Part four. You will hear part of a lecture about the history of standard time. You now have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Morning, everyone. Today's one of those topics that looks like it's about technology and turns out to be about authority. The clock on your mobile is set from a national standard, and nobody thinks that's remarkable. Two centuries ago it would have looked like an outrage. I'll do the before, then the imposition, then the resistance.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, the before. Every town kept its own time, and that wasn't sloppiness on anybody's part. It was astronomy. You set the town clock at the moment the sun stood highest over your own church tower, and that gives you local solar time. Perfectly accurate, and slightly different in every valley.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And the gaps were wider than students expect. Kellwood, which is only a couple of hundred kilometres inland, ran about eleven minutes behind the capital. Sorry — eleven is Merridge. Kellwood is further west again. Kellwood ran sixteen minutes behind, and a traveller crossing both lost a quarter of an hour without doing anything.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: All of which was perfectly liveable while the fastest thing on the road was a horse. It stopped being liveable the moment somebody tried to print a timetable. A timetable has to make one statement about when a train departs, and you cannot do that in a country with four hundred separate noons.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So the companies imposed one. And the reason they could impose it is that the wire ran beside the track. A signal went out from the observatory every morning down the telegraph, and each station pulled its clock into agreement as the signal arrived. It's the wire that made this possible, not the railway.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: On the trains themselves the arrangement was cruder. Each service carried one watch, in a locked case, and it wasn't the driver who held it, because drivers had rather a lot on. It was the guard. That watch was legally the train's time, and if it drifted, the guard paid the fine.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: A quick digression, because it's my favourite document in the whole subject. There's a diary from a stationmaster at Halstow who spent four years writing to head office about a clock that was, by his own account, forty seconds out. Four years of letters. They never once replied. Anyway, back to the argument.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Here's what I want you to notice. By the time anybody legislated, the thing was already done. Railway time crossed the country in about a decade, and for most of that decade it had no legal standing whatsoever. It was a private arrangement that the whole population had simply started obeying.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Right. Four consequences now, and they're printed as sentences on your sheet. This is where the resistance comes in, and the resistance is the part worth your attention. I'll say the number before each one, so keep your pen level with my voice; each one lands in a single clause.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: First. Towns fought it, and they weren't being sentimental about the sun, whatever the newspapers said at the time. What they objected to was who was doing the setting. A private company was now telling a borough council what hour it was, and nobody had voted on that anywhere.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Second, and this is my favourite object in the story. During the changeover, public clocks in a good many towns were fitted with two minute hands? One showed the town's own time and the other showed the railway's, and you read whichever one applied to you.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: Third. Parliament was, as usual, last. The question was actually settled in the courts, in a dispute about when a public holiday began, because it started at midnight local in one town and midnight railway in the next. After that judgement the legislation was a formality.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: And fourth, the one I'd like you to sit with. We did not adopt a national clock because it suited human beings. It doesn't, particularly. We adopted it because it suited trains, and everything since — the shift, the school bell, the tram — has been organised around a standard built for rolling stock.

lines.speaker: s1
lines.text: So, three things to take away. The problem was the timetable, the mechanism was the wire, and the authority belonged to nobody in particular. Next week, the working day, which is the same story with the clock pointed at people instead of engines.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part four. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt:
STANDARD TIME
Before the railways
- Each town set its clocks by local ______ time, taken from the midday sun.
questions.explanation: A printed noun follows the gap, so predict its describing word. 'That gives you' is her naming phrase, and she uses it once. The printed 'midday sun' has already told you what the word must mean, so this is a confirmation rather than a discovery.

questions.prompt: - Kellwood's clocks ran about ______ minutes behind the capital.
questions.explanation: The printed unit fixes this as a bare figure in the tens. She gives eleven, then corrects the place rather than the number: eleven belongs to a different town. The figure attached to Kellwood is sixteen. Write digits and nothing else.

questions.prompt: - Local time became unworkable as soon as railways had to print a ______.
questions.explanation: 'Print a' forces a singular countable document, which rules out every abstract noun in the section. 'It stopped being liveable the moment' announces the turning point. She names the document and then explains why it cannot work. One word.

questions.prompt:
The imposition
- A single time could be distributed because the signal travelled by ______.
questions.explanation: 'Travelled by' wants a means, not a place. Her printed word signal is spoken, but the wire is described before it is named. She then rules the obvious answer out in the last clause: it's the wire that made this possible, not the railway.

questions.prompt: - On board, the one official watch was carried by the ______.
questions.explanation: 'Carried by the' wants a singular job title, so predict a person. She names the wrong one first, gives a reason for excluding him, and only then says it was the guard. One unstressed 'wasn't' is doing all the work here.

questions.prompt: - For most of its first decade, railway time had no ______ standing at all.
questions.explanation: A printed noun follows the gap, so predict its modifier, and the printed 'no' tells you the word describes an authority the arrangement lacked. 'Here's what I want you to notice' is her strongest emphasis marker. The phrase is repeated almost verbatim.

questions.prompt: Towns objected less to the new hour than to the fact that it was being set by a ______.
questions.explanation: 'Set by a' wants a singular institution. She names the wrong motive first and rejects it: they weren't being sentimental about the sun. The objection is about who, and the two-word phrase arrives at the start of the next sentence.

questions.prompt: During the changeover many public clocks were fitted with two ______.
questions.explanation: 'Two' before the gap fixes a plural noun, so the -s is decided before she speaks. She flags the sentence as her favourite object and then describes the thing before explaining it. Her voice rises at the end of that clause, which is a checking-in tone here, not a question.

questions.prompt: The question was finally settled not in parliament but in the ______.
questions.explanation: The frame cancels parliament, so predict a different institution, plural in this sense. 'Parliament was, as usual, last' is the contrast marker. The case she describes turns on a public holiday starting at two different midnights.

questions.prompt: The lecturer's closing point is that the national clock was adopted because it suited ______.
questions.explanation: 'Suited' wants a plural noun for whoever benefited. She offers human beings in the same construction, denies it in three words, and then repeats the frame with the real answer. The sentence structure is identical both times, which is the trap.
