paragraphs.text: A peat bog looks like poor ground. It grows little that anyone can sell, it will not carry a tractor, and for most of the last three centuries it was treated as land waiting to be improved. Underneath the surface, however, lies one of the largest stores of carbon on land. Peat is not soil in the ordinary sense. It is plant matter that has failed to rot, laid down layer on layer at a rate of about a millimetre a year. A bog two metres deep has therefore been building for roughly two thousand years, and the carbon in it has been out of the air for that long. Northern countries hold most of the world's peatland, because cool summers and steady rain are the conditions the process needs.

The mechanism is simple and depends entirely on water. When a plant dies in a dry field, fungi and bacteria break it down within a season or two, and the carbon it holds returns to the atmosphere. In a bog the dead plants sink into standing water instead. Below the water table there is almost no oxygen, and the organisms that do the fastest decay cannot work without it. What decay there is proceeds slowly and stops early. The result is an accumulation rather than a cycle. Sphagnum moss, the plant that dominates most northern bogs, makes the conditions still more difficult by acidifying the water around it, which slows the surviving microbes further.

Draining a bog reverses all of this in a few seasons. Ditches cut to dry the surface lower the water table, and air reaches peat that has been sealed away for centuries. The old plant matter begins to decompose at last, and the bog turns from a place that absorbs carbon into a place that releases it. The peat surface also sinks as it dries and shrinks, so the ditches have to be deepened, which lowers the water table again. Across the uplands of Britain and Ireland, millions of hectares were drained in this way between the 1940s and the 1980s, mostly for sheep grazing and for planting conifers on ground that had never carried trees.

Establishing what a particular bog is doing now is harder than it sounds. The standard instrument is the dipwell, a perforated tube sunk into the peat in which the water level can be read by hand or by a logger. Water-table depth is a good proxy for whether peat is gaining or losing carbon, and it is cheap enough to measure at many points. Direct measurement of the gases is done with sealed chambers placed on the surface, or with a tower carrying an instrument that samples the air many times a second and works out the net exchange over the field around it. Cores taken with a narrow auger give the long record, since the depth of a dated layer fixes the rate at which the peat below it accumulated.

Restoration begins by putting the water back. Contractors work along the old ditches installing dams, built from peat blocks cut on site, from plastic sheet piling or from bales of heather, until the channel is a chain of shallow pools rather than a drain. On bare peat, where the vegetation has gone entirely, the surface must also be covered, since dry peat blows away and washes off in rain. Crews spread cut heather brash over the ground and plant plugs of sphagnum through it. Conifers planted during the drainage years are felled and, increasingly, their stumps are turned over so that the furrows they left do not go on carrying water off the site.

How quickly the benefit arrives is a genuine question. The water table rises within months of the dams going in, and the loss of carbon slows accordingly. Rebuilding a functioning bog surface takes far longer: sphagnum spreads at a few centimetres a year, and a site that has been bare for decades may need twenty years of cover before it behaves like a bog again. There is also a complication that restoration schemes rarely advertise. Wet peat produces methane, a gas that traps heat far more effectively than carbon dioxide over a short period, and a newly rewetted site can emit more of it than a drained one. Most assessments conclude that the carbon dioxide saved outweighs the methane released, but the balance takes years to turn positive.

The money now follows a different logic from the one that dug the ditches. Restoration is expensive, since clearing trees, blocking ditches and revegetating bare ground on a large upland site runs to a few thousand pounds a hectare, and the landowner gains nothing directly from carbon that stays underground. Voluntary carbon codes have grown up to bridge the gap, certifying the emissions a project avoids and allowing a company to buy that reduction. The arrangement is criticised on the grounds that avoided emissions are not the same as removed ones, and that the estimates depend on a counterfactual nobody can observe. It has nevertheless paid for most of the restoration carried out in the last decade.

paragraphs.text: Concrete is the most used manufactured material in the world, and it cracks. Some cracking is unavoidable: the material shrinks as it cures, it moves with temperature, and it is deliberately designed to crack in tension so that the steel inside it can take the load. The trouble is what a crack lets in. Water carrying chloride from de-icing salt or from the sea reaches the reinforcement, the steel corrodes, and corroded steel occupies more space than sound steel, so the surrounding concrete is pushed apart from within. By the time the damage is visible from outside, the repair is structural rather than cosmetic. Across the life of a bridge or a tunnel, maintenance of this kind commonly costs more than the original construction.

Concrete already repairs itself to a small degree, and always has. A batch never fully reacts: grains of cement in the interior stay unhydrated for years because no water reaches them. When a crack opens and rain gets in, those grains hydrate at last and the products of the reaction grow into the opening. Dissolved calcium in the pore water also combines with carbon dioxide from the air and deposits calcium carbonate along the crack faces. Engineers call this autogenous healing. It is real, it costs nothing, and it is severely limited: it closes cracks of about a fifth of a millimetre and no wider, and it works only where water arrives often enough to keep the reactions going.

The best known attempt to extend that process borrows from biology. Certain bacteria survive in strongly alkaline conditions and form spores that stay viable for decades without food or water. Mixed into the wet concrete together with a calcium-rich nutrient, usually calcium lactate, the spores lie dormant in the hardened material. A crack lets in water and oxygen, the spores germinate, the bacteria consume the nutrient and deposit calcium carbonate as a by-product, and the deposit seals the opening. Laboratory work has closed openings close to a millimetre wide by this route, roughly five times the width that autogenous healing can manage. The bacteria then exhaust the nutrient and return to the spore state, ready for the next time water arrives.

The difficulty is the packaging. Spores and nutrient cannot simply be stirred into the mix, because the alkalinity and the crushing that goes on inside a mixer destroy most of them before the concrete has set. They are therefore enclosed in capsules of clay, glass or polymer. This creates a requirement that works against itself: a shell tough enough to survive the mixer is often tough enough to survive the crack as well, and a shell that breaks readily at the crack rarely reaches the crack intact. There is a second penalty. Capsules are weaker than the aggregate they displace, so the more healing agent a mix carries, the lower its strength, and beyond a few per cent by volume the remedy begins to cost more than the fault.

Three other approaches avoid the packaging problem in different ways. Superabsorbent polymers swell when they meet water and plug the crack physically, then draw water in to feed the ordinary reactions around them; they are cheap and act within hours, but they leave a soft pore behind when they dry. Vascular systems run hollow fibres through the element and pump a sealing agent along them. That is the only approach that can be refilled, and the only one that survives repeated damage in the same place, though the network must be designed into the structure and cannot be added later. Shape-memory tendons take a different route again: a strand cast into the beam is heated after cracking, contracts, and pulls the crack faces back together mechanically, which no chemical method can do.

Evidence is where the field is thinnest. Almost all published results come from small laboratory specimens cracked to a chosen width under controlled conditions and then stored in water. Recovery is reported in two quite different currencies. One is regained tightness, measured by how much water or air passes through the specimen afterwards, and it is the figure that matters for durability. The other is regained strength, measured by loading the specimen to failure a second time, and it is the figure that sounds impressive. A specimen can recover almost all of the first and very little of the second. Field trials are rare, because a structure has to be built, damaged and then watched for a decade. The Norland viaduct panels, cast in the mid-2010s with three competing systems side by side, remain one of the few long comparisons anybody has.

So the case is economic before it is technical. A self-healing mix costs somewhere between a tenth and a half more per cubic metre than an ordinary one, which is trivial against the cost of reaching a leaking tunnel lining and irrelevant against the cost of a garden wall. The technology therefore belongs where access is expensive and failure is slow: marine works, buried pipes, deep foundations, the underside of long-span decks. A second obstacle is duller and probably larger. No accepted standard yet says what a designer may assume, so an engineer who specifies a self-healing mix must still design as though it will not heal, and pays for the additive without being allowed to bank the benefit. Until a code recognises the property, the material improves and the design does not.

paragraphs.text: Everything a rocket has ever left in low orbit is still there, or was until it fell. The region between two hundred and two thousand kilometres up holds several thousand working satellites, as many dead ones, several thousand spent stages, and something over a hundred million fragments larger than a millimetre. What makes the fragments dangerous is not their size but their speed. Two objects meeting head-on close at nearly fifteen kilometres a second, and at that speed a fleck of aluminium the size of a grain of rice carries the energy of a grenade. Shielding can be built against the smallest particles. Against anything above about a centimetre nothing useful can be built, and the only defence is to move.

The debris was not mostly made by collisions. Until recently the great majority of catalogued fragments came from explosions: a spent upper stage left in orbit with residual propellant and a charged battery is a pressure vessel that eventually fails, and each failure scatters hundreds of pieces along its own orbit. Two events in the late 2000s changed the arithmetic. One was a deliberate destruction of a satellite by a missile; the other was the first accidental collision between two intact satellites. Between them they added more trackable objects than the previous four decades of spaceflight, at altitudes where the air is too thin to pull them down for centuries.

The theoretical worry is older than either event. The rate at which objects collide rises roughly with the square of how many of them there are, while the rate at which the atmosphere removes them does not, so there is a population above which the debris field feeds itself: fragments produce collisions, collisions produce fragments, and the total climbs even if every launch stops. The cascade, as it is usually called, was set out by the orbital analyst Ruth Delane, who has argued for two decades that certain shells near nine hundred kilometres passed that threshold long ago.

Not everyone reads the models the same way. The aerospace engineer Piotr Renwick accepts the mathematics and rejects the conclusion, since the projections assume nothing changes: no manoeuvring, no disposal, no replacement of a broken satellite by one that leaves when it is finished. The insurance economist Hana Norland is less interested in the physics than in the incentives, and observes that no operator has ever paid for the debris it created, so the models forecast the behaviour of people who face none of the costs. The space lawyer Tomas Verdon notes that an object in orbit remains the property of the state that launched it, whatever condition it is in, so nobody may remove another country's derelict without permission. The astronomer Iris Marlow, whose interest is the sky rather than the traffic, argues that the discussion has been framed too narrowly around collision risk and says nothing about the brightening of the night sky by reflective objects.

Knowing where anything is turns out to be the binding constraint. Ground radar and optical telescopes hold orbits for objects down to about ten centimetres, roughly forty thousand items. Below that size the population is estimated rather than tracked, and it is the untracked centimetre-scale debris that operators fear most, since it can destroy a spacecraft and cannot be avoided. Even for catalogued objects the predictions are coarse: a warning of a close approach arrives days ahead with an uncertainty measured in hundreds of metres, so most warnings are false alarms. Operators manoeuvre anyway, and they are right to, since each burn costs fuel that would have extended the mission but the alternative is losing the spacecraft altogether.

The agreed remedy is to stop adding. Guidelines drawn up in the 1990s ask operators to vent propellant and discharge batteries at end of life, and to remove a satellite from the crowded region within twenty-five years of finishing its work. Both are voluntary, and compliance with the disposal rule has run between a third and two-thirds of eligible missions, improving as regulators have begun attaching the requirement to launch licences. Passivation, the cheaper measure, has been far more widely adopted, and the explosion rate has fallen accordingly.

Removing what is already there is harder in every respect. A derelict stage tumbles, has no fitting designed to be grabbed, and may be leaking. Demonstration missions have caught targets with nets, harpoons and robotic arms, so the engineering is no longer the obstacle; the cost is. A single removal is priced in tens of millions, and the modelling consistently shows that pulling down a handful of the largest, most collision-prone objects each year does more for the long-term population than sweeping up a thousand small ones. I find that conclusion persuasive, and I notice how little it has changed a public conversation still fixed on the image of a vacuum cleaner in space.

What is missing is not technology, and not agreement about the physics. It is a mechanism that makes anybody responsible. A derelict belongs to its launching state and imposes its costs on everyone else, which is the oldest shape in economics. Deposits refunded on disposal, insurance priced against debris, a removal fund: all have been proposed and none adopted. Until one is, the guidelines will do useful work at the margin, and the population will go on being decided by how many satellites are launched rather than by how carefully they are retired.

paragraphs.text: Ask which animals pollinate the crops and the wild plants of a temperate country and almost everyone answers bees. Bees are worth the attention: they are numerous, they are easy to watch, and a hive can be moved to an orchard and counted. But the count is taken during the day, because that is when observers are awake. Moths are harder to study for reasons that have nothing to do with their importance. They fly at night, most species look alike to anyone but a specialist, and they cannot be kept in a box beside an orchard. A different set of insects is at work between dusk and dawn, and until recently almost nobody was counting it.

A moth does not forage like a bee. It has no colony to provision and no store to fill, so it visits flowers for its own fuel and moves on when it has enough. It finds them mainly by smell, following a plume of scent upwind, and the flowers that depend on it advertise accordingly: pale or white petals that show up in low light, a strong sweet odour released after sunset, and a narrow tube of nectar reachable only by a long tongue. Because a moth hovers rather than lands, pollen collects on its head, its legs and the underside of its body, where a casual observer would not think to look.

Counting what happens in the dark has needed three methods, none of them new but all of them recently cheaper. The first is to catch moths at light traps, swab the pollen from their bodies and identify the grains under a microscope, which is slow and demands a specialist. The second, which has changed the field, is to sequence the pollen instead: a short section of plant DNA is enough to name the species it came from, and one machine can process hundreds of samples in a day. The third is to watch. Cameras triggered by movement and lit by infrared record what visits a flower and for how long, without the light that would itself alter the behaviour.

The results have been consistent enough to be surprising. Pollen loads on night-flying moths regularly carry grains from a wider range of plant species than loads taken from daytime visitors in the same field, and marked individuals turn up further from where they were released. Both patterns hold across the studies that have measured them. The two findings fit together, since an insect that ranges widely and visits many species moves pollen between populations that daytime insects keep apart. The night shift is not, on this evidence, a substitute for the day shift. It is a different service, and the plants that receive both do better than the plants that receive either alone.

The pressure that has attracted most attention is light. A streetlight draws moths out of the vegetation and holds them, sometimes for hours, in a column of illumination where they neither feed nor breed. Experiments comparing lit and unlit plots have measured fewer visits to flowers under the lamps and, in several trials, a measurable drop in the seed set of the plants growing there. The effect depends on the lamp. White light with a strong blue component attracts far more insects than the older orange lamps it replaced, which is an unwelcome consequence of a lighting change made for other reasons entirely.

Light is not the largest pressure, however, and the researchers who study it say so themselves. Adult moths need nectar, but a moth population is limited by what its caterpillars can eat, and caterpillars are far fussier than adults. Most species will feed on only a handful of plants, often only one. Hedgerows removed, verges mown before the plants have set seed, and grassland reseeded with a single grass have taken those food plants out of the landscape over sixty years. A garden full of nectar-rich flowers feeds adults very well and adds nothing at all to the next generation.

What follows from this is a set of measures that are cheap rather than dramatic. Lamps can be shielded so that they light the ground and not the hedge, shifted towards the warmer end of the spectrum, and switched off for part of the night, all of which have been done somewhere and none of which costs much. Verges can be cut later and in rotation. None of it will matter unless the caterpillar food comes back, and that is a question about how land is managed rather than about how it is lit. The honest summary is that we know what to stop doing rather more clearly than we know what the benefit will be.

paragraphs.text: A great deal of the energy a country uses ends as warmth that nobody wants. It leaves through cooling towers, exhaust stacks, ventilation grilles and the back of every refrigerator, and in most industrial economies the total is larger than the amount of heat used to warm buildings. The obstacle is not quantity. It is temperature. Heat is only useful at or above the temperature you need it at, and most waste heat leaves at thirty or forty degrees, which is warmer than a room and far too cool to send down a pipe to one. The arithmetic that follows from that single fact governs everything about the systems built to recover it, and explains why a country can throw away more heat than it uses and still find recovery hard.

A heat network is the machine for moving it. Insulated pipes carry hot water from a central source out to buildings and back again, and each building has a substation, a heat exchanger about the size of a wardrobe, in place of a boiler. The temperature the network runs at governs almost everything else about it. The first systems, laid in the middle of the last century, circulated water above ninety degrees, which made them simple to design and expensive to run, since every metre of pipe loses heat in proportion to how much hotter it is than the ground around it. Modern networks run cooler, and the newest designs circulate water at little more than the temperature of the soil and let each building lift it as required.

Once the network temperature falls, sources that were useless become usable. Sewers hold water that rarely drops below twelve degrees even in winter, and a heat exchanger set into a large sewer can serve several hundred flats. A data centre rejects almost all the electricity it draws as warm air, continuously and predictably, which is the profile a network likes best. Metro tunnels accumulate heat from braking trains. Supermarket refrigeration, flue gas from a bakery, the cooling water of a small foundry: none of these is a large source by itself. The point is not that any one of them is impressive but that a network can take several at once, and that a mixture is steadier than any single supply.

Most of them need a heat pump to be worth anything. A heat pump moves heat from a cooler place to a warmer one using electricity, and its efficiency is the ratio of heat delivered to electricity consumed. That ratio depends almost entirely on the lift, the gap between the temperature of the source and the temperature required. Raise water from twelve degrees to fifty and the machine may deliver four units of heat for one of electricity. Raise it to eighty and the same machine may deliver barely two. This is the argument for running a network cool: it is not the pipes that benefit most, it is the pumps.

The economics are decided in the trench. Pipework is the dominant cost of a heat network, and it is a cost per metre, so what matters is how much heat is sold along each metre of route. Planners call this the linear heat density, and it explains the geography of the technology: terraces, tower blocks, hospitals and university campuses are viable, and streets of detached houses with large gardens are not, whatever the ambitions of the people living in them. The same arithmetic explains why new districts are cheaper to serve than old ones. Laying pipe into a street that has already been built costs several times what it costs to lay it before the street exists.

The customer's position is unusual and it is not always comfortable. A household connected to a heat network cannot change supplier, because the pipe goes to one place and a second network to the same street would be absurd. It is a natural monopoly at the scale of a few streets, and it has often been built without the regulation that other monopolies attract. The complaints that follow are consistent across countries: prices that rise faster than the alternatives, long outages with no obligation to compensate, and standing charges that make a small flat expensive to heat. Regulation has arrived in several places, late, and mostly after the complaints.

The constraint that decides most schemes is duller than any of this. A network is a fifty-year asset and the source has to be there for most of that time. A data centre may be rebuilt or moved within fifteen years; a factory may close; a sewer will not. Schemes that have lasted are the ones built on a source nobody can take away, or on enough separate sources that losing one is survivable. That is a planning judgement rather than an engineering one, and it is the reason a technology with no scientific difficulty at all has spread so unevenly. The lesson drawn by the engineers who have built them is that the pipe is the easy part.

paragraphs.text: More is recorded now than at any time in history, and less of it can be read than at any time since paper. The phrase usually reached for is the digital dark age, and it does real damage, because it suggests a single catastrophe that will arrive rather than a slow attrition that is already under way. Nothing is going to go dark. Material is going to become gradually more expensive to retrieve until, for most of it, nobody pays. The distinction matters because the two stories point at different work. A catastrophe calls for a rescue; attrition calls for a budget line that nobody has to defend again each year.

Three failures are routinely run together and they have nothing in common. The first is the medium: a disc oxidises, a tape stretches, a drive fails, and the bits are simply gone. The second is the format: the bits survive perfectly and no software will open them, because the program that wrote them was withdrawn and its specification was never published. The third is the hardest and the least discussed. A file arrives with no record of who made it, when, from what, or why, and it becomes unreadable in a sense no amount of engineering can repair, because what is missing is not the data but the account of what the data is.

Two strategies compete for the second problem. Migration converts a collection into a current format at intervals, which keeps it openable and loses something at every conversion, since no two formats encode the same thing in the same way. Emulation preserves the original files and rebuilds the environment that read them, which is faithful and expensive and pushes the problem back a layer, because an emulator is itself software that will need preserving. Practitioners argue about the balance and agree on the principle: whichever is chosen has to be chosen repeatedly, and an archive that has not converted or rebuilt anything for twenty years is not a stable archive but an unopened one.

The routine work is unglamorous and mostly arithmetic. Every file is checksummed when it arrives, and the checksum is recalculated on a schedule so that silent corruption announces itself before it spreads into the backups. Copies are held in several places, on different kinds of storage, under different administrators, on the principle that failures which are independent are survivable and failures which are correlated are not. Audits check that the copies still match, that the media are still readable and that somebody still knows the password. None of this is difficult. All of it has to continue. The discipline of it is the whole of it, and the failure mode is not a dramatic loss but a year in which nobody ran the check.

That last sentence is where the money is. Building an archive is a project with an end, and every institution knows how to fund a project. Keeping one is an obligation with no end, and the accounting instruments for that are poor. Endowment models exist, in which a sum is set aside whose income covers storage for ever, and they depend on assumptions about return and about the cost of storage decades ahead that no one can defend for long. Costs per terabyte have fallen for thirty years, which invites the assumption that they will keep falling and that the problem solves itself. The staff costs have not fallen at all, and in a mature archive they are most of the bill.

It follows that nothing can be kept indiscriminately, and the profession has always known it. Appraisal, the deliberate decision about what is worth the cost, is the oldest skill in archives and the one that transfers least comfortably to material arriving by the terabyte. The web is the extreme case. A crawl is a sample, taken at an interval, of pages that change between visits, and what it captures is neither the site as it was on any particular day nor the site as its readers experienced it. That is a genuine limitation and not a fault of the crawlers, and it is routinely misdescribed as one.

Opinions differ about what to do with that. The archivist Helen Ashfield argues that the discipline's habit of describing every gap as a technical shortfall has been costly, because it invites solutions that are engineering rather than editorial and postpones the selection decisions that actually determine what survives. The computer scientist Adam Sandmouth takes the opposite line: format specifications should simply be deposited by law when software is sold, which he says would dissolve the second failure entirely. The economist Nadia Brackenfield is unimpressed by both, and points out that the binding cost is neither format nor selection but the wage of the person who checks the checksums, which no legislation and no appraisal policy reduces.

Ashfield seems to me plainly right, and Brackenfield's objection does not weaken her case so much as price it. What is preserved will be what somebody chose to preserve and went on paying for, which has been the condition of every archive that has ever existed and is not made new by the technology. The digital difference is speed. A neglected paper collection deteriorates over a century and can be rescued in its eightieth year. A neglected digital collection is unreadable in fifteen and there is nothing left to rescue.

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists work to a rule that a settlement tells you less about itself than its rubbish does. A house is built to be looked at, and a grave is furnished by people who know that their neighbours are watching. A rubbish heap is edited by nobody. Whatever went into it went in because it had stopped being useful, and it was covered by the next day's waste without ceremony and without arrangement. The heaps have a name of their own in the discipline. A midden is any accumulated deposit of domestic waste, and middens have been dug from coastal shell mounds to the back yards of nineteenth-century terraces.

A midden grows from the bottom up, and that is the property which makes it worth excavating. Each tipping episode leaves a thin layer, and the layers pile in the order they were made, so the deepest material is normally the oldest. Excavators record these layers as separate contexts and lift them one at a time. The sequence is rarely tidy. Animals burrow, children dig, a wall falls into the heap, and a later pit may cut down through forty years of deposit in an afternoon. Reading a midden is therefore a matter of working out which disturbances happened when. Only then can an object in it be trusted to belong where it was found.

Dating a layer usually depends on the least valuable thing in it. Pottery is the standard, because kitchen wares changed shape and decoration steadily and cheap vessels were replaced often. A layer holding a type of jug that was made for only thirty years can be placed within a generation. Glass bottles and clay pipes do the same work for more recent periods. A coin, when one appears, gives a date before which the layer cannot have formed. What a coin does not give is the date the layer did form, since coins stay in circulation for decades and the worn ones circulate longest.

The material that survives is not the material that was thrown away, and the gap between the two is the oldest problem in the field. Bone, shell, pottery, glass and metal endure in most soils. Cloth, basketry, leather, wooden handles, feathers and the greater part of what a household ate do not. A midden dug from ordinary dry ground therefore records a version of daily life weighted heavily towards the hard and the fired. The bias is predictable enough to be corrected for in part, but only in part. Every correction rests on an assumption about how much of the original waste has gone.

Two conditions suspend the usual decay. Permanently waterlogged deposits shut out the oxygen that most decomposing organisms need, and very dry deposits deny them water. At Verdon, a silted ditch on the edge of the old town held water from the medieval period onwards. The excavation there recovered leather shoe soles cut down for reuse, the seeds of at least sixty plants, and large quantities of beetle remains. Of the three kinds of find, the beetles proved the most informative. Different species live in stored grain, in stable litter and in standing water. Their proportions describe the immediate surroundings of the ditch more closely than any of the objects did.

No excavation removes everything, and the choice of what to keep shapes the result more than most published reports admit. Deposits are usually sieved, and the size of the mesh decides which bones come through. A ten-millimetre mesh recovers cattle and sheep and loses almost every fish. When sites began to be sieved at two millimetres, the recorded share of fish in coastal diets rose sharply. It rose because of the mesh rather than because of anything the inhabitants had done differently. Column samples are now taken as a matter of routine for the same reason. A narrow block of deposit is lifted intact and processed in a laboratory.

What a midden cannot supply is people. It can describe a household's consumption across several decades with a precision no document of the period approaches. It can show a change of diet or of fuel inside a single generation. It cannot say who did the eating, and it is often unclear how many households contributed to one heap. Where a yard was shared, and in the crowded districts of the industrial towns most yards were, the waste of six families may lie in a single deposit. Some excavators treat a backyard midden as the record of one household unless there is a reason to think otherwise; others regard that assumption as unsupportable. The argument has not been settled, and it matters, because almost every statement about a household's standard of living begins with it.

paragraphs.text: For most of its history the market of a provincial town happened in the street. Stalls were pitched against the church wall or along the widest thoroughfare, they were struck at dusk, and what remained was mud and refuse. In the middle decades of the nineteenth century a new building appeared in town centres to put an end to that arrangement. The covered market hall was a permanent roof, usually of iron and glass, thrown over a fixed grid of stalls. Within two generations it had become as ordinary a feature of a provincial centre as the town hall or the railway station.

The halls were built with borrowed money, and this fact governed everything about them. A corporation raised a loan and repaid it from the rents of the stalls and from the tolls it charged on goods entering the building. It also had to show the ratepayers a surplus at the end of it. Architects were therefore instructed to fit in as many stalls as the roof would carry. Aisles are narrow in these buildings not because their designers misjudged the crowds but because every metre of aisle was a metre that earned nothing. The accounts were public.

Their family resemblance has a mundane explanation. Cast-iron columns, roof trusses, glazing bars and even the ornamental brackets were ordered from foundry catalogues, in standard sizes, by post. A borough surveyor in Norland could specify a roof that had already been erected at Sandmouth and would be erected again at Ashfield the following year. The parts arrived by rail ready to bolt together. Where local pride demanded difference it was bought at the front, in a stone facade in whatever style the council preferred, while behind it the shed was identical to a dozen others.

What the roof also bought was supervision. Trading in the open had been almost impossible to regulate: weights could not be checked, meat could not be inspected, and a seller who was warned in one street simply moved to another. Inside a hall with named tenancies and a superintendent at the door, all of that changed. The prospectuses of the period lean heavily on cleanliness and on the quality of what was sold, and the argument was not merely rhetorical, since the same decades saw the first serious powers to seize unfit food. Whether health or revenue mattered more to any particular council is rarely recoverable from the minutes.

Not everyone moved indoors. A stall inside carried a weekly rent, and traders who had sold from a basket or a barrow could not raise it or did not wish to be tied to one place. Several towns issued licences for street selling at the same time as they opened their halls, and the licences were fewer than the sellers. The effect was to sort the market: the settled trades took the hall, and the poorest sellers took the surrounding streets, where they were periodically moved on by the same authority that had built the roof.

The halls lost their trade slowly and then quickly. Chains of grocery shops took the packaged goods first. Domestic refrigeration removed the need to buy perishables three times a week, which had been the habit that filled the aisles. The decisive change was the car, because a hall stood on the most valuable ground in the town and had no room to park anything. By the middle of the twentieth century a market hall was often the largest under-used structure a council owned, and a good number were pulled down for shopping precincts and car parks between 1960 and 1980.

The survivors have been rediscovered as architecture. A hall that would have been cleared in 1968 for its site is now listed for its roof, and the arguments made for keeping it are almost entirely about the ironwork. Restoration is expensive, and the money is usually recovered by re-letting the stalls to food counters and independent shops at rents the fishmonger and the greengrocer could never meet. The building is preserved and the trade is not, and traders' associations have said as much at every consultation. Whether a hall without its original tenants is a market or a monument is a fair question, and it is not answered by the quality of the restoration.

It is tempting to file these buildings under public health, and the case is not empty. But the same halls were revenue instruments, and the two purposes were never separated even in the minds of the people who commissioned them. What the century really established was not a standard of hygiene, which arrived by other routes as well. It established an assumption that has outlived every one of these roofs: that trading in a town is an activity to be housed, licensed and given an address. Every shopping centre since has been built on that assumption, and it is worth noticing that it was once a novelty.

paragraphs.text: The age at which a child may lawfully stop attending school has been raised, in most systems that set one, several times over the past century and a half. Each rise followed a similar pattern. It was proposed by a minority, resisted on grounds of cost and of lost family income, and enacted after a delay usually measured in decades. It was then absorbed so completely that within a generation the previous arrangement seemed indefensible. The argument now attaches itself to eighteen in much the language it once attached to twelve. What is striking about the sequence is how little of it turned on evidence about what the additional year does.

Evidence of a usable kind became available only when economists noticed that a change in the law creates something close to an experiment. Two children born a few months apart sit on either side of the date at which a new minimum age took effect. They are alike in almost every respect except the amount of schooling the law required of them. Comparing their later earnings therefore isolates the effect of the extra year from the family circumstances that ordinarily accompany it. Halloran, working on a reform of this kind, reported that the compelled cohort earned measurably more in middle age than the cohort born just before it, and that the difference survived the obvious adjustments.

Devanney has pressed the standard objection, and it is not easily dismissed. An extra year confers a certificate as well as an education, and employers who cannot observe what a candidate learned may be reading the certificate as a signal of persistence rather than of skill. On that account the earnings gain is real for the individual and largely illusory for the economy, since it comes from moving up a queue rather than from producing more. The awkwardness for both parties is that the two explanations predict almost identical earnings data, and the dispute therefore turns on evidence the natural experiment was never designed to supply.

Okorie has approached the question from a direction the economists tend to skip: what the additional year actually contained. Curricula for a newly compulsory year have generally been assembled at short notice, by people who did not ask for it, for pupils who did not choose to stay. Her account of one such reform describes a first cohort taught a shortened version of material most of them had already covered, in buildings laid out for two-thirds of the number. It is a useful corrective, and it cuts in an unexpected direction. If the extra year lifts earnings even when it is delivered like that, the mechanism is unlikely to be the curriculum.

Compliance is the part of the story that policy documents record least well. Attendance in the added year ran well below attendance in the years before it, and prosecutions of parents rose for perhaps a decade and then fell away. The schools that adapted did so by changing what they taught rather than by enforcing what they had been teaching. Strand's study of a single authority found that the institutions which retained their pupils were those that introduced practical courses early, and that this happened without instruction from the centre and, in two cases, against it. The aggregate attendance figures recovered within a few years, which is why the resistance is so often described as imagined.

There is a less generous reading of the whole sequence, and it deserves a hearing. Raising the leaving age removes a cohort from the labour market at a stroke, which is convenient when work is short, and several of the rises were legislated in years when unemployment among the young was rising fast. Bramwell treats that timing as the operative motive and the educational language as decoration. The correlation is real and the inference is not compelled by it; governments legislate about young people most readily when young people are visible as a problem, and that visibility follows unemployment without any cynicism being required.

Where does this leave the case for extension? The earnings gain survives most attempts to explain it away, but it is smaller than the advocates of each successive rise have claimed, and it has been produced under conditions nobody would have designed. What the sequence does not support is the assumption that governs most of the debate: that an additional year is a quantity, and that more of it is better in proportion. Two reforms adding the same year have produced different results within a single decade, which is hard to reconcile with a view of schooling as a stock that accumulates. The comparison that would settle the matter, between two versions of the same added year, has almost never been made.

The useful question is therefore not whether to keep raising the age but what the last year is to consist of. A year designed as a bridge into work or into further study is a different object from a year that repeats the one before it. The evidence assembled so far cannot tell the two apart, because almost every reform examined has delivered the second while promising the first. Until that changes, a debate about a number will go on being conducted with data that was never about the number at all.

reading.title: Academic Reading Test: Society and History 2

paragraphs.text: The words that last longest in a landscape are usually its names. Buildings fall, boundaries move and languages are replaced. The name of a hill or a crossing is passed from one set of speakers to the next, often by people who no longer understand what it means. A settlement may have been renamed twice and still carry an older word in the name of its river or its high ground. That word can come from a language nobody has spoken there for a thousand years. The study of these names is the closest thing there is to reading a landscape's own memory. Like all memory it is partial and easy to misread.

Most names describe the ground. A crossing point, a marsh, a stand of trees, a narrow valley, a ridge with a particular shape: the great majority of settlement names in any long-inhabited region began as directions. This is the least glamorous class and by far the most useful, because the features are still there to be checked. Where a name means the low crossing and the site is a low crossing, the reading is secure. Where the ground has been drained or built over, the name becomes the only record that the marsh existed at all. Drainage engineers have more than once been surprised by what a name warned them of. The class has a further advantage. Its elements repeat across a whole region, so one secure reading supports a hundred uncertain ones.

A smaller class records a person. These are the names built from somebody's name and a word for a farm, an enclosure or a share of land. They are the hardest class to work with, because the person is almost never recorded anywhere else. The name preserves that an individual held the place and nothing more: not the date, not the size of the holding, not whether the holder ever lived there. Attempts to build a social history out of such names have repeatedly run ahead of what the names can carry. The safest use of them is negative. A district thick with such names was settled by people who divided land into individual holdings, whoever those individuals were.

A third class names a function the place has lost. Mills, beacons, gibbets, toll bars, ferry landings and market crosses all left names behind them, and the name usually outlives the thing by centuries. This is where the evidence is at its most concrete and its most easily misdated. A street called after a toll bar tells you a toll bar stood there. It does not tell you when, and in several towns the bar was taken away before the street acquired the surface it now has. The name is a fact about the past with no date attached.

The fourth class is different in kind, because it describes nothing. Settlers carry names with them, and a name that meant a wooded hollow in the country of origin may be fixed to a treeless plain in the country of arrival. Once transplanted, the name stops recording the landscape and starts recording the migration. Norland in one hemisphere and Norland in another are the same word doing two entirely different jobs. Only the second is evidence about people rather than about ground. Transplanted names also cluster. The clustering is itself evidence, and a group of transplanted names in one district usually marks a single wave of arrivals rather than a series of separate decisions.

Whichever class a name belongs to, the method is the same, and its first rule is never to work from the modern spelling. Names are reshaped by speakers who want them to mean something, so a name whose original element has fallen out of use will drift towards a word that has not. Ashfield may look like a field of ash trees and turn out, in its earliest written form, to be nothing of the kind. The earliest recorded spelling is the evidence; everything after it is commentary. The more sense a modern name makes, the more suspicious a careful reader becomes. The rule holds even when the modern form looks ancient, since a spelling can be made to look old as easily as it can be made to look sensible.

There is a further difficulty that no amount of care removes. A name records the moment somebody coined it, and the earliest surviving spelling records the moment somebody wrote it down. Those two moments may be three centuries apart. Written records begin with administration, which in most regions arrives long after the naming. A name therefore gives a date by which the feature existed and no date at all for when it was named. Practitioners state this limit plainly in their own publications, and it is routinely dropped by the time the results reach a wider audience.

paragraphs.text: Money sent home by people working abroad is one of the largest financial flows in the world and one of the least visible. In several small economies it exceeds foreign aid and direct investment combined, and in a few it approaches a tenth of everything the country produces. Yet it is under-recorded almost everywhere, because it arrives in thousands of small sums to households rather than as one payment to a ministry, and a good deal of it never passes through a bank at all. Economists call these transfers remittances. The households that receive them call it the money, and the difference in vocabulary is a fair indication of how differently the two parties see the same flow.

How the money travels has changed twice in a generation. Informal networks, in which a trader accepts cash in one city and an associate pays it out in another, still handle a large share of the flow, and they are cheap, fast and unrecorded. Formal transfer companies charge more, and most of them charge per transaction rather than as a share of the sum, so the smallest transfers carry the heaviest charge. The last decade pulled in two directions at once. Costs fell sharply along the routes that mobile transfer reached, and rose along the routes where compliance rules tightened. A bank that finds a corridor expensive to monitor tends to withdraw from it altogether rather than price the risk.

The oldest argument about remittances concerns what they are spent on. Critics have said for decades that the money goes on consumption rather than investment: better food, a tiled roof, a wedding, a motorbike. The reply is that a roof is a capital good, that school fees buy earnings twenty years out, and that a motorbike in a district with no bus service is working equipment. The standard categories were built for national accounts, and they record a school fee as consumption, so the size of the investment made from this money is understated by construction. That does not settle the argument. It does mean that the figures cited in it are answering a narrower question than the one being asked.

One property of the flow is unusual enough to have changed how economists describe it. Private investment leaves an economy that is in trouble; remittances rise when the home economy falters, because a sender responds to need rather than to return. After a harvest failure or a currency collapse, transfers to the affected region typically climb within a quarter, while portfolio investment has already gone. The flow grows in exactly the years when other money is leaving. That is a valuable property for a household and an awkward one for a statistician, since it means the flow cannot be modelled as investment without producing the wrong sign on every shock.

The costs of the arrangement are borne where they are hardest to count. A household that receives money has also lost an adult, often for years at a time. Ibarra's survey of one rural district found that the care of the children fell almost entirely on grandmothers and elder sisters, and almost never on anyone paid to do it. The same survey found that the households which fared best were not those receiving most but those in which the absence was fixed in advance and known to be temporary. Uncertainty about the date of return, it concluded, cost the household more than any sum the transfers were worth.

Return migration carries a second set of expectations. Policy documents assume that people come back carrying skills acquired abroad, and some of them do. But a bricklayer who has spent nine years on high-rise sites returns to a district that grows fruit, where nobody has any use for the trade he has learned. The equipment he trained on does not exist within two hundred kilometres. Nor are returners a random selection of those who left. People come back because a contract ended, because a parent fell ill, or because the work did not go well. The composition of the returning group is settled by those reasons rather than by anything a scheme can adjust.

Governments have spent twenty years trying to capture the flow. Diaspora bonds, matching schemes that add a public contribution to a private transfer, tax exemptions and dedicated savings accounts have all been offered, and take-up has been modest almost everywhere they have been tried. The explanation most often given is poor design, and some of the designs have indeed been poor. A simpler explanation is available. The money is a transfer between households, sent for reasons that are specific to a family and legible only inside it. A policy that treats it as a national resource is asking a private decision to answer a public question. That is not a design fault. It is a category error, and it is repeated in every new scheme.

paragraphs.text: For about half a century, beginning in the closing years of the nineteenth, the most confident position in design was that applied ornament was a fault. The claim did not begin as a matter of taste. It began as a claim about honesty and about waste, and it was argued in the language of morals long before anyone tried to argue it in the language of appearance. Reformers wrote of decoration as something a serious object could be cured of. That vocabulary is worth noticing, because a fault can be removed while a preference can only be disagreed with, and much of the campaign's authority came from treating its own preference as a diagnosis.

Three separate objections were usually run together. The first was economic: ornament consumed labour that produced nothing, and the labour was underpaid. The second was structural: a carved bracket or a moulded cornice disguised how a building or a cabinet actually stood up, and a viewer who could not read the construction could not judge it. The third was temporal: decoration is dated by the year it was made in a way that a plain surface is not, so an ornamented object becomes unfashionable while a plain one merely becomes old. Each of these is a different argument with a different kind of evidence behind it, and almost nobody separated them.

The economic objection is the easiest to test and the weakest of the three. By the time it was being made most loudly, machine production had already made the repetition of a moulding cheaper than a plain surface finished to the same tolerance. Carving one bracket by hand is expensive; running five hundred metres of the same profile is not, and the profile does not have to be perfect, because the shadow hides the joint. The labour argument was out of date on the day it was made. What survives of it is a narrower point about the conditions under which some hand ornament was produced, and that point is about employment rather than about decoration.

Lindholm has argued that the campaign was in substance about class. Ornament, on this reading, was what the newly prosperous bought when they had money and no inherited vocabulary for spending it, and the reformers who attacked it were marking a distance between themselves and those buyers. The claim is not absurd, and it explains the tone of the pamphlets, which is often contemptuous in a way a purely technical argument does not require. The evidence for it is uneven, however. It fits the pamphlets much better than it fits the buildings, and several of the plainest early works were commissioned by exactly the buyers the reading says were being kept out.

Trewin has restated the second objection in a form that survives scrutiny, and it is the version worth keeping. The target, on this account, was never decoration but pretence. A moulding that pretends to carry a load, a veneer laid to imitate solid timber, a bolted joint concealed to look pegged: these are the objects the argument was built for. A printed pattern that admits to being a printed pattern was never dishonest, because it makes no claim about structure at all. Read that way, the campaign is not against ornament, and a good deal of what was stripped out in its name was stripped out through a misreading of it.

What the campaign produced in practice was not the absence of a style but the arrival of an expensive one. A plain surface has nowhere to hide. Joints must be flush, fixings concealed, tolerances held to a fraction of what a carved surface would forgive, and the finish must be even across a whole plane. The labour did not disappear. It moved from the carver to the fitter, and in several documented cases the plain scheme took longer on site than the ornamented scheme it replaced. Plainness, once it had become a style, also dated, which the third objection had promised it would not.

The reassessment began quietly and is now general. Ornament returned first as printed and woven surface, where the honesty argument had never had any purchase, and then as pattern in materials that make no structural claim of their own. Conservation bodies that had once permitted the stripping of decorated interiors began to refuse it. The question under discussion is no longer whether decoration is permissible, but which of the two, the plain object or the ornamented one, is the more candid about how it was made. That is a question the original reformers would have recognised, even though the answer has moved a long way from the one they expected.

It is a mistake to score the campaign by counting mouldings. Its lasting achievement was not the disappearance of ornament but a change in what a designer is required to defend. Before it, an element could be present because elements of that kind were customary; after it, everything on a drawing has to survive the question of what it is doing there. That question can be answered by a pattern as readily as by a bracket, and the reformers would have denied it, which is the ordinary fate of arguments that win. The habit outlasted the doctrine, and the habit was the valuable part.

paragraphs.text:
A

Bioluminescence is the production and emission of light by a living organism. It occurs widely across the natural world, from glowing fungi on a forest floor to the flashing lanterns of fireflies, yet it is in the ocean that the phenomenon is most common. Scientists estimate that the majority of animals living in the open sea below a few hundred metres are capable of producing their own light. On land the ability is comparatively rare, but in the deep ocean, where sunlight never reaches, glowing bodies are the rule rather than the exception. Most of this ocean light is blue, the colour that travels furthest through seawater.

B

The light is the result of a chemical reaction. In most species it involves a light-emitting molecule called luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase. When luciferin reacts with oxygen, in a process controlled by luciferase, energy is released in the form of light. Crucially, almost none of this energy escapes as heat, which is why biologists describe the glow as "cold light". An ordinary light bulb, by contrast, wastes most of its energy warming the air around it.

C

For many creatures, light is a language. Fireflies are the most familiar example: males and females flash to one another in patterns that are unique to their species, allowing them to find a suitable mate in the dark. Each species has its own rhythm of flashes, and a female will respond only to the correct sequence. In this way light functions much as birdsong does, advertising an individual's identity and availability to potential partners.

D

Other animals use light to hunt. The deep-sea anglerfish carries a glowing lure on a stalk above its mouth; smaller fish, drawn towards the light in the darkness, swim straight into its jaws. The cookie-cutter shark is thought to glow in a way that disguises its outline while leaving a small dark patch resembling a tiny fish, tempting larger predators close enough to bite. For these hunters, light is simply bait.

E

Light can also save a life. When attacked, some squid eject a cloud of glowing material instead of dark ink, confusing a predator while the squid escapes into the gloom. Many small sea creatures use a trick called counter-illumination: they glow faintly on their undersides so that, seen from below, their silhouettes disappear against the dim light filtering down from the surface. Still others light up suddenly to startle an attacker, or to summon an even larger predator that will threaten the animal attacking them.

F

Bioluminescence has proved valuable to people as well. The genes responsible for light production have been transferred into other organisms so that researchers can watch processes that would otherwise be invisible. By attaching a luminescent tag to a virus or a cancer cell, scientists can follow its movement through a living body. Such techniques have become a standard tool in medical and biological laboratories around the world.

parts.title: The Hidden Life of Urban Trees

paragraphs.text:
A

Walk down almost any city street and you will pass them without a second glance: the trees planted along pavements, in squares and in parks. For most of the twentieth century, urban trees were treated as decoration, chosen for their appearance and little else. Today, however, researchers and city planners increasingly regard them as essential infrastructure — as important to a healthy city as its roads, pipes and power lines.

B

One of the most valuable services trees provide is cooling. On a hot day, the air beneath a mature tree can be several degrees cooler than the air above nearby concrete. Trees achieve this in two ways: their canopies cast shade, and they release water vapour through their leaves in a process called transpiration, which lowers the surrounding temperature much as sweating cools the human body. In dense neighbourhoods with few trees, summer temperatures can climb to dangerous levels, a problem known as the urban heat island effect.

C

Trees also clean the air. Their leaves trap microscopic particles of pollution from vehicle exhausts, and they absorb some harmful gases. The benefits are not only physical. Studies have repeatedly found that people who live on streets lined with trees report better mental health, and patients with a view of greenery from a hospital window tend to recover more quickly than those who look out onto a bare wall.

D

Less obviously, trees help to manage water. When rain falls on a city, it runs off hard surfaces and can overwhelm drains, causing floods. A tree intercepts rain on its leaves and branches, and its roots help water soak into the soil instead of rushing away. Some cities have calculated that their trees save millions in flood-control costs each year, and that houses on tree-lined streets sell for noticeably higher prices.

E

Yet life in a city is hard for a tree. Its roots are often squeezed into a small pit beneath the pavement, starved of water and air. Salt used to melt winter ice damages the soil, and passing vehicles pollute the air and physically wound trunks. As a result, a street tree in a busy centre may live only a fraction of the lifespan it would reach in a forest. Planting a tree is therefore only the beginning; keeping it alive demands continuing care.

F

Recognising all this, a growing number of cities have set ambitious targets to expand their tree cover. The most successful schemes share a common feature: they treat trees as long-term assets to be maintained and measured, not as ornaments to be planted and forgotten. Some now give each tree a digital record, tracking its size, health and the value of the services it provides, so that the urban forest can be managed as carefully as any other public asset.

paragraphs.text:
A

Every normally developing child learns to speak, and does so with remarkable speed. By the age of five, and without any formal teaching, most children command thousands of words and an intricate system of grammar. How they achieve this so quickly, from the limited and often messy speech they hear around them, is one of the great puzzles of human development, and it has divided scholars for decades.

B

One early and influential answer came from the behaviourist B. F. Skinner. He argued that children learn language in the same way they learn any other behaviour: through imitation and reinforcement. A child who copies a word correctly is rewarded with attention or with the object it names, and so repeats the behaviour. On this view, the mind of a newborn is essentially a blank slate, and language is built up gradually from experience.

C

This explanation was challenged in the late 1950s by the linguist Noam Chomsky. He pointed out that children constantly produce sentences they have never heard before, and that they make systematic errors — such as saying "goed" instead of "went" — which they could not have copied from adults. Chomsky concluded that the human brain must come equipped with an innate capacity for language, a kind of built-in template that he called Universal Grammar. For Chomsky, children do not so much learn grammar as grow it, guided by a programme present from birth.

D

Several observations are often cited in support of an inborn ability. Children pass through the same broad stages in the same order, whatever language they are learning. They acquire complex rules effortlessly, at an age when they still struggle with far simpler tasks. And there appears to be a critical period: children who are not exposed to any language in their first years find it extremely difficult, perhaps impossible, to achieve full fluency later.

E

More recently, the psychologist Michael Tomasello has offered a different emphasis. He does not deny that humans are specially prepared for language, but he argues that the key lies in social interaction rather than in a grammar template. From their first months, infants share attention with adults — following another person's gaze, or pointing at objects together — and it is through these shared social moments, Tomasello claims, that meaning is first established. Language, on this account, grows out of the human drive to cooperate and communicate.

F

Most researchers today reject the stark choice between "nature" and "nurture". The modern consensus is that children are born with powerful learning abilities that are not necessarily specific to language, and that these interact with a rich social environment. Few scientists now defend Skinner's claim that imitation alone is enough, but few accept every detail of Chomsky's template either. The debate has shifted from whether biology matters to exactly how biology and experience work together.

G

This research is not merely academic. It shapes how we treat children who are slow to talk, how second languages are taught, and how much we worry about the speech that surrounds infants. If shared attention matters as much as Tomasello suggests, then talking and reading to very young children, and responding warmly to their attempts to communicate, may be among the most useful things a caregiver can do.
